Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 1:
The Hymn Entitled the *Adhyardhaśataka* (The One Hundred and Fifty Verses)
Composed by Ācārya Mātṛceṭa (*Prasādapratibhodbhava* = *Śatapañcāśatka* of Mātṛceṭa).
1. Introduction.
Homage to the Buddha.
He in whom all faults are entirely and at all times absent,
and in whom all virtues reside through every possible means.
If one possesses discernment, it is right to go for refuge to him alone, to praise him, to worship him, and to abide by his teaching alone. (BuSto 1.2)
Those defects, along with their latent predispositions, do not exist in the Protector, who is one;
all those qualities of the Omniscient One exist in him, and they are never-failing.
For even one who is intent upon the actions of mind, speech, and body cannot find any opening in the Blessed One, for he is in accordance with the Dharma.

Thus, having attained this human state— a great festival of the true Dharma that is comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke floating upon the great ocean— (I must not let it go to waste).
How shall I not make this eloquence— which follows upon impermanence, which is full of doubt regarding the gaps in karma, and which has its essence extracted— fruitful?
Thus, although the qualities of the Sage have innumerable objects,
an attempt is made to describe even a single portion of them out of respect for my own purpose.
Homage be to you, O Self-Existent One, whose deeds are abundant and marvelous,
and for whom there is no certainty regarding your qualities, whether by way of number or power.
There is no end to them such that one could say "they are this many," so what talk can there be of their being "like this"?
Yet, regarding their virtues, we are merely loquacious in calling them "meritorious."
The first chapter, titled "Praise of the Introduction. Regarding the "Praise of the Cause":
having set aside the deliberation as to whether [the object] is endurable or unbearable, [one proceeds].
This world, which has no one to cry out for help, has been surrendered by you of your own accord.

You are a saint who requires no solicitation; you are affectionate without cause; you are a friend to those with whom you have never been acquainted, and a kinsman to those who have never asked for one.
Even your own flesh was given away; what need is there to mention other things? O virtuous one, you honored those who sought your favor even at the cost of your life.
By you, hundreds of times, the bodies and the life-breaths of embodied beings— seized by those wishing to kill them— were purchased at the cost of your own bodies and life-breaths.
Not out of a desire for some desired state of rebirth, nor out of fear of the two miserable destinies,
but solely through the purity of your intention, you have made ethical discipline your very second nature.
Through the constant abandonment of crooked actions and the constant cultivation of upright ones,
you have become the sole path to the complete purification of all deeds.
By you, whose mind was ever virtuous, even while being repeatedly oppressed by afflictions, your inner splendor was revealed and suffering beings were shown compassion.
The joy that arose in you when you sacrificed your life for the sake of others—
that could not belong even to living beings when their lost lives are recovered.
O Lord, that compassion which arose within you toward even those beings who were your executioners, when you were being repeatedly cut apart and indifferent to the pain— [that is what we seek].
O Hero, you alone are the knower of the essence of that jewel of the mind, which is the seed of perfect enlightenment; other people are far removed from it.
"Without performing difficult deeds, this rare state is not attained";
thus did you cultivate vigor, disregarding your own self.

There has never been for you any fixed rule regarding the excellence of specific qualities; therefore, within you, the sequence of degrees among those qualities—superior, intermediate, and inferior—is severed.
Even toward meditative absorptions that are exceedingly pleasant and fruitful,
you had no attachment, for you were constantly bound by great compassion within your heart.
O one of noble conduct, that pleasure which is not shared with others— even if it is refined— only afflicts those like you and does not truly benefit them.

From the mixed [speech], you have extracted the essence; everything pure has been drunk by you. Well-spoken words have been accepted by you, while ill-spoken words have been avoided like poison. (BuSto 1.24)
O knower of the essence of jewels, you have striven for awakening through various births, acquiring well-spoken words even at the cost of your own life.
Thus, by striving in this manner for three incalculable eons,
accompanied only by your resolve, you have attained the unsurpassed state.
The second chapter, titled "Praise of the Cause.
3. Praise of the Incomparable: Having felt no envy toward those who are superior, and having not looked down upon those who are inferior;
Without engaging in rivalry with your equals, you have attained preeminence in the world.
Your attachment was directed toward causes and not toward fruits;
therefore, through that correct practice, all virtues reached their perfection in you.
In such a way have you led your self to excellence through your virtuous deeds,
that even the dust of your feet has attained the status of a sacred shrine.
Having attenuated the faults and then extracted them, and having increased the virtues and purified them, you have attained supreme perfection through that excellent method.
In this way, you have struck at the faults with a total assault,
such that not even a trace of their latent predispositions remains within your own mental continuum.
Having thus repeatedly gathered and accumulated these qualities within yourself,
not even a semblance of them is seen elsewhere.
Every worldly object used for comparison is subject to impairment and obscuration, limited in time, localized, and possesses qualities that are easily surpassed. (BuSto 1.33)
What comparison, then, can there be for your qualities, which are free from duality, inaccessible, eternal, irreversible, and unsurpassed?
The depth of the salt ocean becomes as shallow as a cow’s footprint when your own intellectual depth is observed to be bottomless and boundless.
The stability of the earth becomes as light as the tip of a *śirīṣa* petal when your own stability—
unshakable among all phenomena— is made manifest.
O Sage, within the sphere of your light of knowledge— which destroys the cataract of ignorance—
the sun does not find even a foothold, let alone the glow of a firefly.
In comparison with the purity of your speech, intellect, and conduct, even the purities of the autumn moon, the sky, and the waters seem to attain a state of impurity.
By this, everything that is good in the world has been explained;
for the worldly dharmas of poor ascetics are far indeed from the dharmas of the Buddhas.
O virtuous one, by the very attainment of that jewel of the Dharma through which you have reached preeminence,
your equality with it is established solely by that alone.
But when something that is merely a deceptive pretense of one's own desire is introduced under the guise of a general or subtle point, that is the excessive fickleness of the speaker. (Bu-ston 1.41)
The third chapter, titled "Praise of the Peerless.
4. Praise of the Marvelous:
Indeed, as I contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I perceive it as if it were being expanded.
And the entire world has been won over by you toward the victory over Māra.
For even when great fury is aroused against them, those who strive to strike back find no burden too heavy for patience— especially when that patience is established within a worthy vessel.
That very great destruction of the afflictions which occurred immediately after the defeat of Māra was accomplished on that very same night; that indeed is most wonderful.
O Hero, whoever would feel astonishment at the sun, garlanded with a thousand rays, dispelling the darkness, would likewise feel astonishment at your victory over the heretics.
The lustful one is conquered by the one free from lust; the wrathful one, by the one who has overcome anger;
and the deluded one, by the one free from delusion—thus are the three always conquered by these three.
You praise the true Dharma and censure the false Dharma;
yet for you, there is neither attachment to the existent nor aversion toward the non-existent.
Since your mind feels neither aversion toward the Arhats nor attachment toward the heretics, what praise could there be for you?
There was no attachment even toward virtues, nor any craving even for those possessed of virtue;
oh, how pure is this being who is so well-composed!
Through the constant clarity of your faculties, which never departs at any time,
your mind is eternally serene and appears as if directly perceived.
Those purities of intellect and memory are well-known even to children;
they have been made manifest by your well-spoken words and noble deeds, which reveal your inner state.
The Fourth Chapter, titled "Praise of the Marvelous. 5. Praise of Form:
It is peaceful and lovely, radiant and unimpeded.
To whom would this form, both serene and majestic, not captivate?
Whether it be one who has seen it a hundred times or one who beholds it for the first time,
your eye finds equal delight in that form for both of them.
For because of its marvelous nature and its gentle character,
your body produces ever-new delight at every single sight.
Your body is endowed with the qualities of its substratum, and your virtues with the qualities of their possessor;
you are possessed of a supreme excellence that is mutually harmonious.
Where else could these qualities of a Tathāgata be well-established,
except in this very body, radiant with the primary marks and secondary signs?
"Fortunate am I"—thus your form seems to speak, as it were, to the virtues you have taken up; "We are well-placed"—thus those virtues seem to answer in return. (BuSto 1.57)
The Fifth Chapter, titled "Praise of Form. 6. Praise of Compassion:
This entire world is, without distinction, bound by the afflictions.
Out of compassion, you have long been bound for the sake of liberating the world from its afflictions.
Whom should I first revere: you, or great compassion—that very [compassion] by which, despite knowing such faults, you have remained for so long in saṃsāra?
When those times passed while you were occupied with the habituation to the bliss of solitude,
that which was done by your compassion has now found its opportunity.
From the peaceful forest, you are indeed drawn toward the edge of the village out of compassion for those to be trained, like a nāga being pulled from its lake by a spell.
Although you abide in supreme tranquility, being moved by the power of compassion,
you have set foot even upon the arts of the actors and musicians.
Whatever miraculous powers you have, whatever lion’s roars, and whatever manifestations of your own virtues—
these are the whetstone for your compassion, which has cast off the subtle tendencies of desire.
O Protector, compassion— which is solely for the sake of others and entirely auspicious— though it may be harsh toward its own locus, has become compassion only in you alone.
For in this way, having divided you into a hundred parts like an offering, the wise ones have scattered you throughout the directions for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.
Indeed, by your very will, she proceeds manifestly in accordance with you;
for even while obstructing you, she, being virtuous, does not commit an offense.
The sixth chapter, titled "Praise of Compassion.
7. Praise of Speech: Your words are well-phrased, of great significance, truthful, and sweet.
They possess meanings that are both hidden and manifest, and they are characterized by both conciseness and elaboration.
Upon hearing such words as these from you, who could not be certain that you are omniscient, even if they were directed against you? (BuSto 1.68)
Generally, everything is sweet, though by necessity some things may be otherwise;
yet, because of the accomplishment of your purpose, every single word of yours is well-spoken.
Whether it be gentle, harsh, or endowed with both qualities,
all of your speech attains a single flavor upon reflection.
Oh, how supreme is the skill of these perfectly pure deeds,
by which such a vessel has been fashioned for these jewels of speech!
For from this mouth of yours, which is as beautiful to the eye as ours, these words flow forth, enchanting to the ear, like liquid nectar flowing from the moon.
Your speech, which pacifies the dust of passion, acts like a rain-cloud;
and with respect to the extraction of the serpent of hatred, it acts like the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa).
It acts once more as the sun, dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
it acts as Indra’s weapon, utterly shattering the mountains of pride.
Your speech is unfailing because its meaning is evident; it is unconfused because it is free from afflictions;
it is persuasive because it is well-composed; indeed, your words possess the three excellences.
First, your words captivate the minds of listeners;
then, when they are reflected upon, they dispel both passion and ignorance.
Your speech carries the yoke of yoga: it provides consolation to those in distress, terror to the heedless, and spiritual urgency to those who are complacent in their happiness.

This speech is a source of joy for the learned, an enhancer of the intellect for those of middling capacity, and a dispeller of the darkness of ignorance for the dull-witted; it is thus universal in its appeal.
Your speech draws one away from [wrong] views, draws one toward nirvāṇa, extracts faults, and rains down virtues.
Your intellect is unimpeded everywhere, and your mindfulness is present in all circumstances;
therefore, every one of your explanations is fruitful in every respect.
Since you do not exert yourself toward an unworthy place, nor at an improper time, nor with an unfit recipient,
your speech is unfailing, like vigor that has been correctly initiated.
The seventh chapter, titled "Praise of the Words. 8. Praise of the Teaching:
It is the sole path, a means to happiness, continuous, and free from harm.
Your teaching is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end; no other's is so.
Thus, if fools, out of attachment to their own views,
revile that which is entirely beautiful to you, there is no enemy equal to such a view.
Reflecting upon the many calamities that have befallen this world for his sake, you should remain steadfast even in the face of adversity within his teaching.
How much more so, then, should you carry out the teaching of one who acts for your benefit and speaks for your benefit—even if your head were ablaze! How could it not be done?
Freedom, the bliss of awakening, the honoring of your qualities, and peace—
all this fourfold excellence is attained through your teaching.
O Hero, this teaching of yours terrifies all the non-Buddhist heretics, torments Namuci, and brings comfort to gods and men.
By your teaching, the great ground of the three realms— unimpeded and unrestrained— the very dominion of Death itself has been overcome.
For one who knows the method of your teaching may remain even for an eon by his own will;
yet, being independent, he goes wherever death has no jurisdiction.
The division of time into the three periods— of reflecting on the meaning of scripture, of meditative cultivation, and of veneration— exists nowhere else except in your teaching.
O bull among sages, what indeed could be more calamitous than this, that they do not honor the teaching thus endowed with excellence?
The eighth chapter, titled "Praise of the Teaching. 9. The Praise of the Vow:
Hearing [your teaching] satisfies, and seeing you inspires serene confidence.
Your speech brings delight; your teaching brings liberation.
Your birth gladdens you; your growth delights the wise;
your activity bestows favor, while your withdrawal brings harm.
Chanting [your name] removes sin; remembering you brings joy;
seeking you develops the intellect; and full realization is purifying.
Approaching you brings prosperity; serving you brings supreme wisdom;
honoring you brings fearlessness; and attending upon you brings auspiciousness.
Pure through the perfection of ethical discipline, serene through the perfection of meditative concentration,
and unshakeable through the perfection of wisdom— you are a great lake consisting of merit.
Form is the jewel to be seen by you; well-spoken words are the jewel to be heard;
the Dharma is the jewel of investigation; for you are indeed a mine of jewels of virtue.
You are the island of refuge for those whose selves are wounded by being swept away by the torrents [of saṃsāra];
you are the shelter for those afraid of existence, and the ultimate resort for those seeking liberation.
Because of your pure conduct, you are a worthy recipient; because of the abundance of your fruit, you are a fertile field;
and because you act for the benefit of all living beings, you are a true friend.

You are beloved because of your helpfulness; you are captivating because of your excellence in pleasure; you are exclusively charming because of your gentleness; and you are highly esteemed by all for your manifold virtues.

You are dear to the heart because you are irreproachable; you are delightful because of the excellence of your speech and form; you are blessed because all your aims are accomplished; and you are auspicious because you are the refuge of all virtues.
The ninth chapter, titled "Praise of the Vow. 10. Praise of the Entry onto the Path:
You are the one who casts out those who remain [in worldly existence] and the restrainer of those who carry away [the teachings].
He is the restorer of those who have gone astray and the inspirer of those who move sluggishly.
You are the yoker of those who are tamed to the pole, and you are indifferent toward the unruly;
therefore, you are the unsurpassed, true charioteer of men who must be tamed.
Compassion for those in distress, a desire for their welfare when they are healthy,
sympathy for those in calamity, and the wish for the benefit of all.
Affection even toward those who oppose you, engagement even with those who have fallen,
and compassion even for those who are fierce— what indeed is this nobility of yours?
If the status of being a guru is ascribed to one's mother and father because of their helpfulness,
then what of your own guru-hood toward me, who have been so exceedingly beneficial?
Like selfs that are mutually opposed and indifferent to their own purposes,
you have become a rampart for those standing on the brink of a precipice.
For the benefit of both worlds and for transcending the world,
you have created the light of wisdom in worlds shrouded in darkness.
The modes of enjoyment among gods and humans are diverse;
yet, through the commonality of enjoying the Dharma, they have attained non-distinction in you.
O Blessed One, you have indeed established this universal hospitality toward all phenomena, regardless of birth, age, appearance, place, or time.
Those gods, with palms joined in reverence, wait upon even those disciples who are free from longing, though they themselves long for them, appearing as if amazed at those who are unamazed.
Oh, how radiant is the appearance of a Buddha within the circle of saṃsāra,
wherein even human birth has become an object of longing for the gods!
The tenth chapter, titled "Praise of Entering the Path. 11. Praise of Difficulties:
weariness, the loss of the bliss of tranquility, and association with unpleasant people.
Bearing these faults—namely, the pairs of opposites and distraction—as if they were virtues.
Since you strive for the welfare of the world with an unattached mind,
O Blessed One, what indeed is this *buddhadharmatā* of the Buddhas?
Even poor food was eaten; at times, one was afflicted by hunger;
uneven paths were traversed; and one slept even upon the thorns of oxen.
O Lord, although you are the Sovereign, out of affection for those to be trained, you underwent delays and obscurations, and even adopted different dress and speech.
O Protector, although you possess abundance, it is never found within yourself;
for like one who must speak, you are constrained by all to employ yourself freely for their own sake.
By whomsoever you may be urged, wherever, and however,
you do not overstep your own auspicious path of conduct.
People do not act with such benevolence even toward one intent on helping them,
as you act with benevolence even toward one intent on harming you.
Toward an enemy intent on your harm, you are a well-wishing friend intent on your benefit;
though he is constantly seeking out faults, you are devoted to seeking out his virtues.
Since your invitation was accompanied by poison and fire,
your journey there was full of compassion and like nectar.

Those who reviled you have been conquered by your patience; those who harmed you by your blessing; those who spoke falsely against you by your truth; and those who sought to kill you by your loving-kindness.
The many dispositions of human beings, which have been suppressed since beginningless time,
were revealed by you as having fallen into ruin and transformed in a single moment.
The eleventh chapter, titled "Praise of Difficult Deeds.
12. Praise of Skillfulness:
That those who were fierce have become gentle, and that the miserly have attained generosity;
That the cruel have attained gentleness is due to your skill in means.
The pacification of the senses in Nanda, the humility of Mānastabdha, and the forbearance of Aṅgulimāla—who would not be struck with wonder? (BuSto 1.125)
Having abandoned their golden beds, many steadfast ones lay happily upon beds of grass; they were satisfied with the essence of the Dharma.

Though questioned at times, you did not speak; even when approached, you engaged in conversation only after first causing [the interlocutor] to thirst. Thus, knowing the proper time and disposition, you spoke in another world.
Having first generated excellence in the mind through discourses on generosity and the like, the Dharma is then imparted to that stainless person, just as dye is applied to a clean cloth.
There is no means or power by which you have not exerted yourself to uplift this wretched world from the terrible abyss of cyclic existence.
Many words and deeds of manifold forms have been displayed by you here and there, according to the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained.
All these are pure, non-contradictory, honored, and revered;
they are beneficial and magnified for all gods and men.
For it is not possible to both speak and act much and well;
yet both of these are seen in you, O speaker of what is otherwise and not otherwise.
The world would become purified by you through the purification of your own self alone,
for no such field as this exists within the three worlds.
How much more so for those who have utterly perished throughout the beginningless perils of existence— that you alone are thus resolute for the benefit of all sentient beings!
The twelfth chapter, titled "Praise of Skillfulness.
13. Praise of Freedom from Debt: I do not know that path by which there might be repayment to you.
Even those who have attained final nirvāṇa are people who remain indebted to them.
Established in the Dharma, they act solely for their own sake;
as for the labor they undertake for that purpose, what recompense can there be for you?
For you remain awake, observing the continuities of those who sleep;
vigilant among the heedless, you are a kinsman of auspiciousness to all beings.
The destruction of the afflictions has been proclaimed, the illusion of Māra has been dispelled;
the wretchedness of cyclic existence has been described, and the direction of fearlessness has been shown.
What else could there be for one who desires the welfare of beings and acts out of compassion,
wherein you have not already granted your favor?
If these phenomena were migratory, they would certainly have been established by you everywhere, having taken Devadatta as their basis.
For this very reason, O Lord of the World, you have said that here no one is the agent of another, as if making known that the world is merely a manifestation of being.
Having for a long time on earth promoted the true Dharma out of compassion for the world,
and having produced many excellent disciples capable of benefiting the three realms, [he passed away].
Having directly disciplined those belonging to the class of disciples up to Subhadra,
what debt toward sentient beings still remains for you today?
You, who pulverized the bones into pieces as small as sesame seeds with the vajra of meditative concentration,
did not abandon your performance of what is exceedingly difficult even at the end.
"Both my Dharma-body and Form-body exist solely for the sake of others"—
this you have demonstrated even in your Nirvāṇa for this world that is so difficult to instruct.
For thus, having transferred the Dharma-body in its entirety to others,
and having broken your form-body into pieces as small as sesame seeds, you have entered final nirvana.
Oh, what stability! Oh, what conduct! Oh, what form! Oh, what virtues!
Indeed, there is nothing at all among the qualities of a Buddha that is not wondrous.
Even toward you—who are helpful, pleasing to the eye, and whose speech and physical actions are peaceful—people act with hostility; behold the ferocity of delusion!
To those beings who pay homage to you— the ocean of merit, the treasury of jewels, the mass of Dharma, and the mine of virtues— to them also let there be a well-performed salutation.
"O Protector, those qualities of yours are inexhaustible, whereas my power is subject to exhaustion;
therefore, I remain out of fear of such consequences, not because of satiety."
Immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and invisible—
you alone are worthy to know yourself by yourself.
Not even a fraction of a portion of your virtues has been proclaimed, yet supreme satisfaction remains established in our hearts;
for indeed, the thirst of people is quenched by the waters of great lakes without even being drawn out.
By the ripening of this auspicious karma of mine, which arose from the inspiration granted by the grace of the Sage,
may my mind— driven by the wind of unwholesome discursive thoughts— become submissive to the needs of all living beings.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "Praise of Freedom from Debt," is concluded.
The *Adhyardhaśataka* is finished. The work of the master Mātṛceṭa.

If a person, being firm in constant resolve, recites the twelve [verses] of the *Ādibuddha* in the morning, they will surely obtain whatever they desire.

Having prostrated with my head before the Sage with a most serene mind,
I shall today proclaim the names described by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Possessing a beautiful form and assuming all forms, he is indeed the unsurpassed one who is complete in all marks; Mañjuśrī is supreme in glory.
Inconceivable, free from the conceivable, inconceivable with wondrous prowess;
he is inconceivable among all phenomena and likewise inconceivable to the mind.
Your self is cultivated in emptiness, you are endowed with empty phenomena;
you are empty, your resolute conviction is empty, and you are the teacher of the emptiness of the three realms of existence.
The omniscient one, the all-seeing, the sovereign lord of all stages,
the all-pervading Mañjuśrī who wields mastery, the lotus-eyed one, born from the lotus.
Having the color of a lotus filament, seated upon a lotus pedestal,
holding a blue lotus, he is pure, holy, and tranquil in mind.
You are called the Pratyekabuddha, the Buddha, and the Ādibuddha;
you possess miraculous powers, have attained mastery, and are the teacher of the Four Truths.
You are the world-protector, the thousand-eyed one; you are the Lord, the progenitor of beings.
You are Śiva to all living creatures; you are the pervasive one, an ocean of virtues.
You are a meritorious ṛṣi, the most excellent and the eldest, as well as one who remembers his former births;
you are the leader, the guide, the son of the Jina, and the offspring of the Jina.
You are Bhānu, the possessor of a thousand rays; you are Soma and you are Bṛhaspati;
you are Dhanada and Varuṇa; you are Viṣṇu and you are Maheśvara.
You are Ananta, the king of nāgas, and likewise Skanda, the commander of the army;
you are Vemacitra, the lord of the asuras, as well as Bhauma, Śukra, and Budha.

you have transcended the impurities of worldly dharmas and are the foremost person in the world.

the bestower of boons, the shelter, the protection, and the one invincible to the deeds of Māra.
Profound and irreproachable through the excellence of your spiritual friends, you are a physician who extracts the arrow; you are a tamer of men and a skilled charioteer.
He is wise, possessed of movement, intelligent, and discerning;
he is meritorious, a wish-fulfilling tree, adorned with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment.
The basis for all embodied beings is endowed with the fruit of liberation;
it is captivating, pleasing, and faultless for those who lead the holy life.
You are Ketu, the best of the planets; you are the preeminent sage among sages, consecrated as a crown prince, the lord and master of the ten stages.
You are the caravan leader, the best of the assembly, the teacher of supreme nirvāṇa;
you are like space, the intermediate eon, and you are both fire and wind.

homage be to you, O Great Knowledge, who are venerated by all beings!

Homage to her who, with a single glance, draws in the entire host of worldly kings;

who is illuminated by the *vidyā* and the syllable *hūṃ* placed upon the ten-syllable feet.

the wise person endowed with devotion to the Goddess should recite it in the morning with self-restraint. (BuSto 5.22)
Having arisen either in the evening or in the morning, one should remember [the Buddha], who bestows fearlessness upon all,
quiets all sins, and destroys all miserable rebirths.
He shall be swiftly consecrated by seven crores of Victors;
and within just one month, he shall happily proceed to the state of Buddhahood.
Whether it be a most terrible poison, whether stationary or mobile, it does not take hold upon his mere recollection, even if it has been eaten or drunk. (BuSto 5.25)
It destroys the poison of others' wives for those afflicted by the poison of the host of planetary spirits,

One desiring a son shall obtain a son; one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;

therefore, it is certain that even one such as I has been seized by grasping within that [compassion].
And you possess a second power, a solar orb for the fierce darkness of the sins of the entire world.
"I am indeed suffering, yet I still burn with passion; fie, alas! upon this wicked and foolish misdeed!"
Shame, shame on me, unfortunate as I am— who, though the darkness has been dispelled even by the radiance of the sun,
still thirsts at the banks of the Himavat’s river where the rocks are cool with fragments of ice;
who, like a pauper, remains within the interior of a vast jeweled cave-house on the main street of the Isle of Gems.
Having made you, O Blessed One, the sole nurturer of all the world, her who was without a protector, your own protector.
Even a mother cries out for the sake of her milk when her child is ill and falls into distress; even a father harbors anger toward his son who is daily intent upon improper desires.
But you are the supreme creeper upon the great wish-fulfilling tree, which yields the vast fruit of the aspirations of the three worlds.
You bestow upon all those things they have requested, yet you never undergo any transformation whatsoever.
"Whosoever has a body ablaze with the fire of the flood of afflictions, for each of them I am the Savior"—
make this self-conceived vow fruitful for me, who am submerged in the abyss of suffering,
as long as these harsh humiliations and the surges of misery increase for living beings.
Compassion for those whose minds are held by their vows within the vehicle of the perfectly enlightened Buddha lasts only for that long.
Thus, with arms raised high, he cries out a wailing sound under the pretext of words of praise; O Mother, even another person would not deserve to be ignored, how much less one such as you?
For while you behold the prayers for desired prosperity from others, they have already attained their wishes through you.
I am burned even more intensely by an inner fever born of discontent that is difficult to endure.
If I am a sinner, why does this great devotion toward you increase within me?

For by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and even by your name alone, you alone forcibly remove sin; you alone are she who must lay down the burden of activity. Therefore, O You whose speech is truth, tell me how it is so.
Will a physician, possessing vast compassion, refuse to prescribe wholesome medicine even for a patient who is about to die? "Why do you weep? he would ask.
Driven by base qualities such as deceit, envy, and pride, and simultaneously by my own inherent defects, I am like a young elephant in a monastery that shares its portion with many others;
because I do not obtain the worship of your lotus feet for even a moment, for that reason— specifically— [I pray].
May this composition of words and phrases, though humble and piteous, be fruitful for my desire.

From the boisterous, loud laughter of the crashing, bursting, and shattering shorelines tossed beyond their bounds by the playful agitation of waves surging and rolling as the winds of the end of the eon whirl about,
there arose the piteous wailing and cries of those sinking with shattered ships, rendered motionless and faint by their sorrowful lamentations.
O Goddess, by those intent on praising you, the shore of the ocean is reached immediately and at will.

With their beds resting within houses cleared by the force of a fire— terrifying with its crackling flames and leaping sparks that dance upon the lap of the sky-born clouds, which are themselves mistaken for smoke—
their eyes raised in supplication with hands folded in salutation and crowns bowed low, they offer prayers unto you.
In an instant, they are seized by the enemy—the clouds blazing with the play of rising lightning.

Remembering you as death, the elephant— whose body is balanced upon the high swing-like surface of its tusks, whose fire of hatred is provoked by rival elephants summoned by the "hūṃ" cries of the swarms of bees clinging to its temples filled with the water of rut— [perishes].
Seated upon the peaks of the towers atop his broad summits, he responds with great joy.
In the empty forest, where there is a festival of vine-like tridents upon the heads of men struck by the blows of mature spears,

he employs bandits— whose pride is swollen by the flashing sword-blades they grasp with the tips of their hands— as his slaves, merely by being gazed upon with eyes accompanied by frowns and the knitting of curved brows.
The abode of your glories has its syllables clearly inscribed by the stylus of thought, though it was weary from the labor.

The lion, with its sharp fangs and fierce mouth, enraged and desiring to pounce nearby, has its thick mane disheveled as the joints of its broad shoulders are washed by the thick blood dripping from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants torn open by the tips of its claws, which are as hard as vajra-strikes.
Trembling, he turns back and departs with words whose meaning is smeared by the hymns composed for you.

Having united against you from their sinful nature with nooses of serpents— whose faces are pervaded by the activity of a flood of wide hissing breaths and whose forms are distorted by darkness like swirling smoke, and which possess long, flickering tongues for ropes— you, whose self is devoted to nothing but you, become intent on enumerating the multitude of your virtues.
He bears a splendor adorned with a garland of blue water-lilies and a circle of intoxicated bees as his bracelets.
With his hair roughly seized by the fierce soldiers of the army who tremble at the frown of their master,
and bound fast by the harsh noose of knots with the loud clamor of the shouting servants,
he— his throat wasted by hunger and thirst— suddenly abandons that calamity which has such a miserable end.
Whoever would go for refuge to the feet of Noble Tārā, even if abandoned by affectionate kinsmen, [shall find protection].

For one who has removed all evil through the recollection of the mantras extracted from your Tantra, these [powers] bring about an invincible state— though they are formidable with the grand display of rays from weapons corresponding to the undertaking of various false forms and diverse costumes fashioned through the sequence of the activities of illusion and emanation.
Upon the garlands fashioned from the multitude of entrails and strings of intestines threaded through the corpses, the *rakṣasas* provide protection.

At the time of battle, he was obstructed by enemies with powerful arm-strength— enemies who were like roaring clouds in form, creating a darkness of continuous torrents from the threefold pride and passion, whose weapon-rays flashed like lightning, and who rained down a shower of falling arrows.
Nourished by the enthusiasm granted by you, this sole hero violently crushes the earth of his enemies.

Their bodies have their wounds devoured by creatures emerging from the hollows of the openings of channels where putrid pus and foul-smelling blood flow out from diseases uprooted by the persistence of evil conduct;
yet, through devotion, they are intent on the practice of the excellent medicinal pill of service to your feet.
They are born with bodies resembling refined gold and with eyes as broad as lotuses.
He for whom the alms of the sacred tradition (nāyā-bhaikṣya), offered by his gurus into the vessel of his ears,

has found rest; and who, though having attained the mastery of speech enriched by the splendor of all ornaments and adornments, had fallen into a state of muteness in learned assemblies due to the lack of wealth in the Vedas— [he has now become eloquent].
Yet, by the power of devotion to you, he too seizes the lion-thrones of the disputants in the royal assembly.
Sleeping on the ground, grey with dust, his body illuminated by the tattered cloth of his split hip-cloth,

grinding away at the life-spans of lice in a skull-bowl before the swarm of bees, seeking alms while striving to worship you— that man shall attain a beauty as lovely as the smiling fly-whisks borne by choice young women.
The *mūrvī* plant bears a dense mass of teeth from elephants blinded by rut, with its single upraised parasol.
Exhausted by various means such as service, labor, crafts, entreaties, exchange, and stratagems, and failing to obtain wealth—
the fruit of merit accumulated through the store of virtue acquired in previous births— they have now petitioned you, O Earth, the one who transcends fate, for the sake of these wretched people.
Furthermore, the destitute obtain treasures of extinguished gold.
His livelihood cut off, ashamed and being rebuked by his wife whose garment was torn, abandoned from afar by his own kin, children, friends, and relatives because of his self-indulgence,
he shall report his suffering to you regarding houses whose boundaries have been overturned by the tips of horses' hooves.
He exercises his power, awakening from sleep by the jingling sound produced by the bracelets of the women within his inner apartments.
The elephant is one whose broad tusks touch the circle of the horizon and flash with great rays, adorned with the marks of excellence;
the excellent horse has six tusks and hair as dark as a peacock's neck;
the jewel consists of radiant, blazing rays and possesses stainless qualities; and the treasury is a golden storehouse filled with wealth.
By a mere fraction of a portion of your grace, O Blessed One, he becomes a general with heroic troops.

At his own will, the lord of the Vidyādharas— having attained supernatural power through your science— goes to the Malaya forest of honey-fragrance, where he has made an appointment upon a jeweled slab scented with sandalwood water, and where, out of affection for sporting with his beloved, he provides genuine hospitality newly prepared.
His thick, elevated arms, dark as the luster of a sword, shine with glittering bracelets.
Their breasts were adorned with pearl necklaces; their long eyes rivaled the blue water-lilies at their ears;
their hair was braided with jasmine and intoxicated bees by the fragrance of its noble scent;
and the drums of their exquisite anklets resounded loudly, following the continuous melody of their girdles.
The daughters of the gods, joyful with the intoxication of passion, respectfully entreat you as their protector.
[He beheld] a lake with its interior covered by jewels, possessing golden lotus-pools with diamond filaments,
a canopy of pollen shaken by female bees from the rising *pārijāta* trees,
and the sweetness of musical instruments provided by the celestial nymphs of the city of Amarāvatī, who were skilled in the lute and the flute.
Having performed service to you, he enjoys for a long time a journey through the Nandana grove.

With beautiful women sporting in the Mandākinī river— a stream of water with abundant splashes— whose waters were scented by the powder of camphor, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, agallochum, and sandalwood, and wherein the waves rested within the whirlpools of the deep bosoms of their beloveds, swelling with the pride of passion.
They sport, their inner faculties being transformed by the power of intense merit directed toward you.
His commands were saluted by the leaders of the host of gods, whose heads bowed under the weight of humility;
he had ascended the lap of heaven upon the celestial elephant, whose limbs were made radiant by the tinkling of ornaments,
while his body was covered with intense horripilation as it was gently swayed by the creeper-like arms of Śacī.
Purified by the falling glances of your eyes, Hīra protects the divine earth with his unbroken forearm.
The Sugata, seated upon the crest-jewel ornament, is the canopy of celestial glory; he fills the three worlds with rays more intense than ten million rising young suns,
while Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Viṣṇu bow down under the weight of his stance as he stands firmly on one foot in the *ālīḍha* posture.
Your form, when meditated upon, becomes the means for cutting through the fear of cyclic existence for those subject to birth.

Some behold him in a state of wrath, his arms—resembling great staffs emitting rays of weapons—filling the expanse of the sky; his conduct made formidable by the hoods of the serpents encircling him as ornaments; and the violent clashing of his *ḍamaru* drums, which are terrifying to enemies and accompanied by a laugh that strikes fear into the wicked.
Fierce with the tumultuous clamor of great play, intoxicated by the joy of the frantic dancing of the *vetālas*.
Some, however, perceive within the space of each individual pore the entire expanse of the sky and the surface of the earth,
with the Brahmās, Indras, Rudras, and others— humans, gods, siddhas, gandharvas, and nāgas— remaining in their natural states;
they perceive the infinite emanated minds of hundreds of Sugatas stationed in abodes that pervade the circle of all directions.
Wondrous, venerated by the three worlds, it is the intrinsic nature of all states, both stable and moving, without exception.
Some [behold] the redness of the sun with rays reddened by the hue of lac and vermilion;
others likewise [behold it] as blue as the crushed powder of petals from a magnificent, dense sapphire;
some [behold it] as whiter than the milk churned from the Ocean of Milk; and others [behold it] as having the luster of gold.
Your form is the universal form, which, like a crystal, appears divided according to the distinctions of the adjuncts placed near it.
Only the Omniscient One, the sole witness who has revealed the reality of all knowable objects through the lamp of omniscient wisdom,
or his son Sarvavid, can truly comprehend the enumeration of your multitude of virtues;
whereas one like me merely shrieks loudly, gaping with a mouth that rattles like a crow’s.
That calamity is a cause for laughter for a mind afflicted by the pain born of the fever of intense suffering.

That which I am now requesting for the very first time—you who know it especially well—is a procedure involving excessive effort in speech that serves as a cause for the satisfaction of the minds of the ignorant. However, having vomited forth this sorrow through words like poison before a dear friend— [The text continues: ...the wise man, though knowing the truth, does not speak of it; for he knows that even the slightest pain arising from such a disclosure causes distress to the heart of the beloved one. Therefore, O King, you should not be distressed by my words, for they are uttered out of affection. Just as a physician administers a bitter medicine to a patient suffering from disease, so too do I speak these harsh words to you, who are afflicted by the fever of grief, for the sake of your ultimate benefit. Thus, O Lord of the Earth, you should not harbor resentment toward me, but rather grant me leave to depart. For the wise man, having understood the intent of his friend’s speech, should not be angry, but should instead respond with kindness. Even one who knows the truth, being pained, finds as it were a state of well-being through the lightness of heart.

O Dhanakaruṇā, you who are like a digit of the moon manifesting in the ocean of auspicious bliss, bestow your cooling glance; grant nourishment through instructions in wisdom; destroy the darkness within me.
In my mind, purified by the waters of your hymn of praise, you are the sole abode of all that is auspicious.
For it is observed that in this world, even the mere chanting of your qualities by living beings is never in vain.

By whatever merit I have obtained through praising the mass of your qualities— which are beyond measure or limit— and which is sweet with the taste of the fruit of a desire moistened by merit, to be enjoyed until liberation;
by that merit, may the world [be graced] with the auspicious svastika-mark on the soles of the feet of the Noble Lord of the World.
With this merit, may he go forth to that land of the Son of the Sugata known as Sukhāvatī.
The *Āryatārāsragdharāstotra*, composed by Śrī Sarvajñamitra, is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 7:
(Ārya)tārāṣṭottaraśatanāmastotram (The Hymn of One Hundred and Eight Names of Noble Tārā)
Oṃ namaḥ śrī-āryatārāyai.
In the beautiful and glorious Potalaka, resplendent with various minerals,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and echoing with the songs of various birds.
Resounding with the splashing of various waterfalls, teeming with various wild animals,
and perfumed on all sides by various species of flowers.
It resounded with the humming of bees drawn to various heart-pleasing fruits,
with the sweet songs of *kinnaras*, and was crowded with rutting elephants.
Resounding with the hosts of accomplished vidyādharas and gandharvas,
it is constantly and perfectly frequented by sages free from passion.
And by other hosts of bodhisattvas who are masters of the ten stages,
as well as by noble goddesses such as Tārā and thousands of vidyārājñīs.
Surrounded by other hosts of wrathful kings, such as Hayagrīva and others,
the Blessed One Avalokita is intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then the glorious one, seated upon a lotus-womb throne,
endowed with great ascetic power and possessed of loving-kindness and compassion, spoke.
And he taught the Dharma there in that great assembly of gods;
having arrived there, the mighty Vajrapāṇi cast [the thunderbolt] aside.
Endowed with supreme compassion, he questioned Avalokita regarding that place crowded with thieves, serpents, lions, fierce elephants, tigers, and the like.
O Sage, these beings are sinking, submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra,
bound by the snares of worldly existence consisting of passion, hatred, and darkness.
"O Great Sage, tell me that by which sentient beings are liberated.
Thus addressed, the glorious Avalokita, Lord of the World, [replied].
He spoke these sweet and awakening words to the wielder of the thunderbolt:
"Listen, O King of the Guhyakas, to the instruction of Amitābha."
My command, born from the power of my vow, is the mother of the world;
endowed with great compassion, she is raised up for the sake of lifting the world out of its suffering.
Resembling the rising sun and possessing the radiance of the full moon’s face,
she was making this Tārā speak to the gods, asuras, and humans.
Shaking the three worlds and terrifying the yakṣas and rākṣasas, he spoke to the goddess who held a blue lotus in her hand, saying, "Do not fear! Do not fear! (BuSto 7.15).
I was brought forth by the Victors for the sake of protecting the world from wildernesses,
the clash of weapons, and being overwhelmed by various fears.
"By the mere recollection of my name, I always protect sentient beings;
I shall deliver sentient beings from the great ocean of various fears."
Therefore, the bulls among sages sing of me as "Tārā" in this world;
then, with palms joined in reverence, I was filled with respect and trepidation.
As it blazed in the sky, he spoke these words:
"Recite the hundred names that were proclaimed by people in the past."
[This merit] was [taught] by the lords who are masters of the ten stages, the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power;
it removes all sins, is meritorious, auspicious, and increases fame.
It bestows wealth and grain, promotes health and increases nourishment;
it generates longevity and well-being, bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
O Great Sage, relying upon loving-kindness toward all beings, proclaim that which establishes prosperity and fortune and increases the welfare of all sentient beings.
When this was said, Avalokita, the Lord of the World, smiling,
gazed out upon all directions with a vision suffused with loving-kindness.
Raising his right hand, which was adorned with auspicious marks, the one of great wisdom said to him: "Excellent, excellent, O you of great austerity!"
Listen to the names, O highly fortunate one, who are as dear as an only son to all beings;
by reciting which, men shall attain prosperity and become lords of wealth.
Freed from all diseases and endowed with all qualities of sovereignty,
those who have escaped being consumed by untimely death go to Sukhāvatī upon passing away.
I shall proclaim them; O hosts of gods, listen to me!
Rejoice in this, and you shall become perfectly at peace.
Oṃ locane sulocane tāre tārodbhave, you who have compassion for all sentient beings, you who deliver all sentient beings, you with a thousand arms and a thousand eyes!
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One! Look upon me, look upon me!
And for all sentient beings: *huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.

Oṃ, pure one, completely purified one, daughter of the Sugata, whose heart is loving-kindness, stainless one, dark-hued one, you of dark form, possessed of great wisdom, adorned with powerful and excellent ornaments!
Aparājitā, the greatly fierce one, who possesses all forms and great power;
Oṃ Suśriye!
Oṃ! Kalyāṇī, of great splendor, sustainer of the world, of great renown;
Sarasvatī, large-eyed, wisdom, glory, and increaser of intelligence. BuSto_7.29 //
Bestower of fortitude, bestower of nourishment, Svāhā, Oṃ-kārā, she who assumes forms at will;
she is intent on the welfare of all beings, the victorious one who delivers from battle.
The goddess Prajñāpāramitā, the delightful Noble Tārā, Dundubhī, Śaṅkhinī, Pūrṇā, Vidyārājñī, and Priyamvadā. BuSto_7.31 //
Candrānanā, Mahāgaurī, Ajitā, Pītavāsasā,
Mahāmāyā, Mahāśvetā, and she of great strength and prowess.
Mahāraudrī, Mahācaṇḍī, the destroyer of wicked beings;
Praśāntā, Śāntarūpā, Vijayā, and Jvalanaprabhā.
Vidyunmārī, Dhvajinī, Khaḍginī, Cakriṇī, and she with raised bow as her weapon;
Jambhanī, Stambhanī, Kālī, Kālarātri, and Niśācarī.
Rakṣaṇī, Mohanī, Śāntā, Kāntārī, Drāvaṇī, and Śubhā;
Brahmāṇī, Vedamātā, Guhyā, and Guhyavāsinī.
Auspicious, belonging to Śaṅkara, gentle, Jātavedas, swift as thought,
skull-bearing, of great speed, Sandhyā, truthful, and invincible.
She is the caravan leader with a compassionate gaze, who shows the way for those who have lost their path;
she is the bestower of boons, the instructor, the teacher, the one of beautiful form, and whose prowess is nectar.
Śarvarī, Yoginī, Siddhā, Caṇḍālī, Amṛtā, Dhruvā, Dhanyā, Puṇyā, Mahābhāgā, Śubhagā, and Priyadarśanā. // BuSto_7.38 //
