O Great Dharma, supreme among the virtuous Dharmas, the Wheel of Dharma—homage be to you!
O Buddha-being, supreme among excellent beings, being of the Dharma, upholder of the excellent being; highest of beings, knower of the excellent being, being of beings—homage be to you!
O Avalokiteśa, supreme protector, great lord, who beholds all;
O light of light, for the sake of the world, lord of the world—homage be to you!
O you who are the world, the syllable, the non-syllable, the great, the foremost of the supreme syllables,
the non-syllable among syllables, the all-seeing one, the syllable of the wheel— homage be to you!
O Lotus-handed One, Great-handed One, Consoler, Bestower!
O Buddha-dharma, Great Buddha, whose very nature is the Buddha—homage be to you!
O Buddha-form, great form, vajra-form, most beautiful one! O supreme light of the Dharma, most radiant, illuminator of the world—homage be to you!
O Padmaśrīnātha, foremost of lords; O Dharmaśrīnātha, possessor of lords;
O Brahmanātha, Great Brahmā, Son of Brahmā—homage be to you!
O Lamp, foremost of lamps, fierce lamp, light of the lamp,
excellent illuminator, Lord of lamps, great lamp, Buddha-lamp— homage be to you!
O consecrated by the Buddhas, O supreme among Buddhas, O son of the Buddha, O great wise one! O you whose head is the foremost of the Buddhas' consecrations, O Buddha of Buddhas, homage be to you!
O Buddha-eye, Great Eye, Dharma-eye, Great Seer;
O you whose entire essence is meditative concentration and gnosis, Vajra-eyed one, homage be to you!
Thus, by meditating upon or even praising your eight hundred secondary names with one's whole being, one shall attain sovereignty over the world.
The hymn of supplication in one hundred and eight names of the noble Avalokiteśvara is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 17:
The Hymn of the Prayer of Noble Conduct (Bhadracarīpraṇidhānastotra)

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, illuminating for even more eons and successions of eons as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable successions of world-systems and Buddha-fields, made this vow by singing these verses:

"However many lions among men there may be in the worlds of the ten directions, throughout all the three times—I bow to them all without exception, with body, speech, and mind, full of serene faith. (BuSto_17.1)
With bodies as numerous as the atoms of all buddha-fields, I pay homage to all the Victors with a mind directed toward every Victor, through the power of the vow of the *Bhadracaryā*.
Upon every single atom, Buddhas as numerous as atoms sit amidst the sons of the Buddhas;
in this way, I have full conviction that the entire realm of phenomena (dharmatā-dhātu) is filled with Victors.
And within those oceans of inexhaustible praise, with the sounds of oceans of all vocal qualities,
I praise all those Sugatas while proclaiming the virtues of all the Jinas.
With the finest flowers and the finest garlands, with the finest musical instruments, ointments, and parasols,
with the finest lamps and the finest incense, I perform worship to those Victors.
With excellent garments, supreme perfumes, and caskets of powder as vast as Mount Meru,
and with all the most distinguished and sublime arrays, I perform worship to those Victors.
And whatever sublime, unsurpassed worship there may be, I resolve upon it for all the Victors;
through the power of my resolve in the *Bhadracaryā*, I pay homage to and worship all the Conquerors.
And whatever sin I may have committed under the influence of passion, hatred, or delusion—
whether by body, speech, or mind— I confess it all.
And whatever merit exists in the ten directions belonging to those in training, those beyond training, and the Pratyekabuddhas,
as well as to the sons of the Buddhas and all the Victors— that I rejoice in all of it.
And those lamps of the world in the ten directions, who have awakened to enlightenment and attained non-attachment—
I entreat all those Protectors to turn the unsurpassed wheel.

And those who desire to manifest parinirvāṇa, to them I pray with palms joined: may they remain for as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, for the benefit and happiness of the entire world.
Whatever merit I have accumulated through prostration, worship, confession, rejoicing, entreaty, and supplication, I dedicate it all toward enlightenment.
May the Buddhas of the past be honored; may those who currently abide in the worlds of the ten directions, and those yet to come, quickly fulfill their aspirations and awaken to enlightenment.
May whatever realms there are in the ten directions become completely pure and sublime;
may they be filled with Victors seated at the foot of the king of Bodhi trees, and with the sons of the Buddhas.
May whatever beings there are in the ten directions always be happy and free from illness;
may the righteous welfare of the entire world be accomplished, and may their hopes be fulfilled.
And while practicing the conduct of awakening, may I remember my births in all states of existence;
in all lives, through death and rebirth, may I always be one who has gone forth into homelessness.
Training myself in accordance with all the Victors and fulfilling the conduct of excellence,
may I always practice the stainless and pure conduct of ethical discipline, unbroken and without flaw.
By means of the voices of gods, the voices of nāgas, and the voices of yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and humans— indeed,
by all the voices of the world— I teach the Dharma within all those voices.
May those who are indeed devoted to the perfections never lose sight of the mind of awakening;
and may whatever evil obscurations exist be completely exhausted without remainder.
May I wander liberated from karma, from afflictions, and from the path of Māra within the worldly realms,
unstained like a lotus by water and unattached like the sun and moon in the sky.
Pacifying all the sufferings of the lower realms and establishing the entire world in happiness,
may I act for the benefit of the whole world throughout as many paths of fields as there are in the directions.
Following the conduct of sentient beings, fulfilling the conduct of awakening,
and manifesting the conduct of excellence, may I practice throughout all future eons.
May I always meet with those who share my same conduct;
in body, speech, and thought, may I practice the vow of a single way of life.
And may I always meet with those friends who desire my welfare and who show me the way of the *Bhadracaryā*; may I never at any time cause them to be displeased.
May I always behold the Victors face-to-face, surrounded by their sons, O Lords;
and may I perform magnificent worship for them all throughout all future eons without weariness.
Upholding the true Dharma of the Victors, illuminating the conduct of awakening,
and purifying the practice of excellence, may I practice throughout all future eons.
Wandering through all states of existence, he has attained the inexhaustibility of merit and wisdom;
through insight, skillful means, meditative concentrations, and liberations, he shall become an inexhaustible treasury of all virtues.

Upon a single atom there are as many fields as there are atoms; and within those fields, while practicing the conduct of awakening, he beholds inconceivable Buddhas seated in the midst of their sons of the Buddha.

Thus, throughout all directions without exception, within the paths of the ignorant, he enters oceans of Buddhas, oceans of realms, and oceans of practices and eons, as vast as the measure of the three times.

Through the ocean-like sounds of the components of a single voice, may I constantly enter into the purity of the vocal qualities of all Victors and the voices of all Victors according to their inclinations— the eloquence of the Buddhas.
And within those inexhaustible sounds and melodies, may I enter by the power of my intelligence, turning the wheel of the method of all the Victors belonging to the three times.
In a single instant, may I enter all future eons; and those eons whose measure is the three times, may I traverse them, having entered into ten million instants.
And those lions among men who have gone throughout the three times, may I behold them in a single instant;
and may I always enter their sphere of activity through the power of liberation that has reached the state of illusion.
And those arrays of the fields of the three times, he brings forth upon the tip of a single atom;
in this way, he enters without exception all the arrays of the fields of the Victors in every direction.
And those lamps of the world who have not yet appeared— awakening within them to the turning of the wheel,
and reaching the peace that culminates in the manifestation of nirvāṇa— to all those Protectors I shall go.
By the power of supernormal feats with universal speed, by the power of knowledge with universal gates,
by the power of conduct with universal virtues, and by the power of loving-kindness that reaches everywhere.
By the power of merit that is all-pervading purity, by the power of knowledge that is unimpeded,
and by the power of wisdom, skillful means, and meditative concentration, he fully accomplishes the power of awakening.
Purifying the power of karma, crushing the power of the afflictions,
and rendering the power of Māra powerless, may I fulfill all the powers of the conduct of excellence.
Purifying the ocean of fields, liberating the ocean of sentient beings,
discerning the ocean of Dharmas, and plunging into the ocean of primordial wisdom.
Purifying the ocean of conduct, fulfilling the ocean of aspirations,
and making offerings to the ocean of Buddhas, may I practice through the ocean of eons without weariness.
And whatever specific vows for the conduct of awakening belong to the Victors of the three times,
may I fulfill them all without exception, having awakened to enlightenment through the *Bhadracaryā*.
To that wise one, the eldest son of all the Victors, whose name is Samantabhadra,
I dedicate all this merit for the sake of his practice of shared conduct.
May there be purity of body, speech, and mind, as well as purity of conduct and purity of the field;
O Bhadra, may I become equal to that wise one in every respect.
May I practice the *Bhadracaryā*, the universally auspicious vow of Mañjuśrī;
may I fulfill every single one of those actions without exception throughout all future eons, untiringly.
There would be no measure to their conduct, nor would there be any measure to their virtues;
abiding in that immeasurable conduct, I know all their miraculous transformations.
As far as the limit of space may extend, and as far as the limit of sentient beings without exception,
and as far as the limit of karma and afflictions— so far shall the limit of my vow extend.
And those who might give to the Jinas infinite realms in the ten directions adorned with jewels, along with divine and human excellences of happiness, for as many eons as there are atoms in a realm;
And whoever, having heard this king of dedications, should once produce resolute faith while aspiring for supreme enlightenment—this merit would be foremost and most distinguished. (BuSto 17.48)
By him the realms of misery are avoided, and by him evil friends are avoided;
he who has this vow of the *Bhadracaryā* quickly beholds that Amitābha.
Well-gained is their gain, well-lived is their life, and welcome is this human birth for them;
for just as Samantabhadra is, so too shall they become before long.

Whoever, under the influence of ignorance, has committed the five evil deeds of immediate retribution— by reciting this *Bhadracaryā*, they shall swiftly bring them all to complete exhaustion without remainder.
In terms of knowledge, form, characteristics, complexion, lineage, and physical appearance, he is invincible to the hosts of heretics and paths; he is honored throughout the entire three worlds.
Swiftly he goes to the king of Bodhi trees; having gone there, he sits down for the welfare of sentient beings.
He awakens to enlightenment, turns the wheel [of Dharma], and subdues Māra along with his entire army.
Whoever upholds, recites, or teaches this *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna*, the Buddha knows the ripening of that merit here; it is distinguished awakening—do not have doubt, but generate [aspiration for] it!
Just as the heroic Mañjuśrī knows, and likewise Samantabhadra,
following their example, I dedicate all this merit.
Whatever supreme dedication has been praised by all the Victors throughout the three times,
with that I dedicate all this merit toward the excellent *Bhadracaryā*.
And when I am undergoing the act of death, having turned back all obscurations,
may I behold Amitābha face to face and go to that realm of Sukhāvatī.
When I have gone there, may all these vows of mine be fully realized in their entirety;
and having fulfilled them without exception, may I bring about the welfare of sentient beings throughout the world.
There, in that most beautiful and delightful circle of Jinas, he was born upon a splendid and exquisite lotus;
there he received a prophecy directly from the Jina Amitābha.

And having obtained the prophecy, may I, by the power of my intelligence, perform many deeds for the benefit of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, together with many hundreds of millions of emanations.
Whatever slight merit I have accumulated by reciting the *Bhadracari-praṇidhāna*,
may it all be perfected in a single instant, and through that, may the auspicious aspiration of the world be fulfilled.
By the infinite and most distinguished merit obtained through dedicating the *Bhadracaryā*, may the world,
submerged in a flood of calamities, go indeed to the excellent city of Amitābha.
The *Śrī Bhadracarīpraṇidhānastotra* is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 18:
*Bhaktiśatakam* (The Hundred Verses on Devotion)
Homage to that Blessed One, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, whose knowledge has all things as its object and whose speech is faultless— composed by the Great Paṇḍita Rāmacandrabhāratī.

We pay homage to that Blessed One—whether he be the Buddha or Giriśa—in whom not even a trace of passion exists, nor hatred, nor likewise delusion; and whose causeless sweetness of compassion is vast and bestows happiness upon infinite sentient beings. BuSto_18.1 //
Lord Śambhu is not your enemy, nor is Hari your foe; he is neither your adversary, nor is he indifferent, nor is he the Self-born (Brahmā), nor yet others such as Indra and the rest.
The Buddha is not merely a teacher, nor is he a kinsman in this world, nor a father, nor one of the same lineage or the same birth.
But among these, he who is free from passion and all-knowing is the one to be served by the wise.
Brahmā is overcome by ignorance and embraced by the great illusion so difficult to master;
Viṣṇu, out of excessive passion, holds Pārvatī upon his own body;
whereas that Blessed One, the Lord of Sages, is free from ignorance, free from illusion, and devoid of passion in this world.
"Tell me, tell me, O brothers: who among them should be served by the wise for the sake of liberation?"
Having attained in many ways the stations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara through various causes, alas, they wander again in saṃsāra, that abode of absolute suffering.
Of what use are those states for embodied beings— states fraught with misfortune and possessed of a beginning and an end?
Therefore, one should always aspire to the state of a Buddha, which is without beginning, middle, or end.
The form of consciousness is subtle, all-pervading, pure, devoid of external form,
effortless, formless, the seed of boundless compassion,
undecaying, omniscient, free from all limiting adjuncts, and the bestower of immortality through its sovereignty.
May that reality, which is to be resorted to by those who have conquered the bodiless one (Kāma), become my refuge.
Subtler than the subtle, unimpeded by afflictions, infinite, and greater than the great; having conquered the world through his majesty and possessing abundant compassion;
two-armed yet armless, the supreme among bipeds yet footless; the giver of the three [refuges].
Having two eyes yet being eyeless, possessing qualities yet being without qualities—that indeed is my refuge.

Eternal bliss, reality, the heart of aesthetic flavor, the abode of eloquent speech, worthy of service by the virtuous, having perfectly realized the truth, with an equanimous mind, self-established, the goal to be attained, the bestower of all fruits, and possessing a gentle countenance.
May that object of mine, which is beneficial to all and for all, become my refuge.
This [teaching] is self-arisen and possessed of higher knowledge, the remover of the fear of existence, and free from terror;
it belongs to one of radiant fortune, possessing great heroism devoid of worldly enjoyment,
the conqueror of passion, the fourfold path, pure by nature, and likewise without a creator.
May that reality, which is the most excellent in the world, extend its vast joy throughout all realms of existence.
In some places blue, in others yellow, and in yet others red;
in some places with the luster of the moon, and in others beautiful with the hue of madder; in some places possessing a brilliant radiance—thus it proceeds through a variety of colors.
Bearing those various six crests upon that object, it is the refuge.
Impenetrable by others, with a complexion as radiant as Jāmbūnada gold, possessing the three refuges,
the three vehicles, and the three wisdoms, he is the sanctuary for the three worlds and the speaker of the threefold word;
a vessel of compassion, with a gentle smile, wearing a beautiful saffron-colored robe.
Having performed meditation, with feet fixed in the siddhāsana posture, take refuge in the object.
With a serene pair of eyes like blooming blue lotuses, repeatedly expounding the Tripitaka out of compassion for the multitudes of gods and men;
supremely peaceful and equal toward gold, stones, silver, and clods of earth.
May that reality become the refuge for me, providing a fresh hospitality to my eyes.
I go for refuge to the Buddha, the most excellent and virtuous; I follow the Dharma, the foremost among those free from passion;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the preeminent among assemblies.
Furthermore, I go for refuge three times, twice, or thrice.
Once again I go for refuge to the Buddha; once again I honor the Teacher, the Guru of the World.
Once again I speak, I praise, and I bow: O Gautama, there is no satiety in me for you.
Having repeatedly surveyed the three worlds, I have taken refuge in the pollen of the lotus of your feet;
this and this alone is my deity. There is no other refuge for me—no, no, no.
Homage again and again to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, who proclaim that "all is impermanent, suffering, and without self."
O Blessed One, free from passion, I bow to your very feet; O Lord of Sages, thus do I worship you again and again.
Furthermore, I worship you repeatedly, beyond and beyond, on both sides, above, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions.
O Lord of Sages, I bow a hundred times to that holy ford of merit— the path by which you have gone here, and wherever you stood, wherever you sat, and wherever you lay down through the power of yoga.

I bow to that place where the Blessed One himself was born, where he fully awakened to all things, where the Wheel of Dharma was most clearly illuminated, and where the nectar of immortality was filled.

With devotion, I pay homage to the stainless sacred tooth-relic, which possesses a splendor as beautiful as the jasmine and the moon—the royal swan in the lotus-pond of the wheel of the Omniscient One; who is worshipped by the hosts of gods; who is coemergent with the wheel of the sublime Dharma; and who is the Pārijāta tree for the people.

I bow my head to the supreme reliquary of the Victor, which holds the image of the inexhaustible relic placed at the foot of the Bodhi tree upon the peak of the Golden Mountain situated on the Trikūṭa, atop the perimeter of the earth-realm above the abode of the Nāgas.

I bow to that Blessed One who, having attained awakening as the King of Mountains— its base radiant upon the Vajra-throne and its jeweled well within a circle of golden basins— immediately thereafter achieved omniscience through the conquest of Māra.
O head, bow to the Buddha; O ear, always listen to the Dharma spoken by the one who teaches non-duality; O eye, behold everywhere the incomparable form; O nose, smell the lotus feet.
O tongue, praise the Friend of the Sun (the Buddha), and O friend, you should worship the Cloud of Glory (Śrīghana).
O mind, contemplate this: the abode of the Jina at Vajrāṅghri is established as our own virtue.

The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—this triad is a great, priceless jewel. From this day forward, I entrust my very self to these three, which destroy the fear of the three realms of existence for one seeking liberation. May I be devoted to them; there is no other supreme refuge for me—this is the truth.
May I become his disciple; I bow down ten million times to this one praised by the thirty gods.

O Sage, I do not seek gain or honor, nor am I terrified by fear, nor do I desire fame; it is not because you are born of the lineage of Dharmāṃśu that I have come to you for refuge, O Sage, nor out of a desire for knowledge, nor because of tradition; rather, it is because of your universal benevolence.
Having discerned right knowledge, you have set out to cross the ocean of existence.
Having fallen into the ocean of sandalwood paste— the radiance of your various virtues such as dispassion, compassion for all beings, and wisdom— one is unable to go elsewhere;
whether kings punish you, or the wise censure you, or even your kinsmen [do so].
"O Victorious One, Father, I cannot live even for a moment without you."
Whether my dwelling be in heaven, in hell, among the animals, in the city of the asuras,
or in the city of the pretas, or anywhere else by the power of karma— O Omniscient One, may I then and there hear your virtues, which flow like nectar to the ears.
My mind takes refuge in those who are free from evil; I have no other prayer for happiness.
I am indeed your servant, captured by you through the price of my virtues;
I am indeed your disciple, disciplined by you through your own words;
I am indeed your son, having attained that state and finding happiness through the mindfulness [you have bestowed].
O Guru, Lord Buddha, my father, protect me from existence!

You are the father, the mother, the brother, and you are the sister; you are the steadfast friend in adversity, the kinsman, the lord, and the supreme preceptor for initiation into the nectar of immortality.
You are sovereignty, you are enjoyment, you are wealth and grain, and you are majesty.
O Omniscient One, you are my fame, my knowledge, and my very life—everything to me.
O Sage among Sages, free from passion, ocean of compassion, Sugata who has shattered the great cage of existence,
Buddha who has attained the nectar of immortality— O Sinless One, may your fragrant palace abide within the lotus of my mind.

In this wheel of saṃsāra—which is selfless, impermanent, impure, consisting of the suffering of suffering, and without end—you alone are the one capable of protecting me; O Lord, ocean of compassion, therefore be gracious, be gracious, be gracious!

Be gracious, O Lord, Lord of Gods, Lord of the World, Victorious One, praised by the universe, praised by me, praised by the virtuous, Buddha! O non-terrible one, enemy of existence, enemy of passion, enemy of darkness—I am your devotee alone in body, speech, and mind.

He alone is your son of noble family, he alone is your devotee, he becomes the bearer of the burden of your teaching, he is your disciple, he has gone for refuge, and he alone is your servant— whoever does not transgress your command under any circumstances.
O Buddha! Benefiting the world is indeed your worship; harming the world, O Lord of the World, is your affliction.
O Victor! How am I not ashamed to speak thus, being a devotee at your lotus feet, yet having harmed the world? (BuSto 18.33)
Wealth, people, power, your own body, and the kingdom— whatever was given by you a hundredfold for the sake of helping others—
where is my compassion now for this world that harms him who helped you, and where is my joy or even my loving-kindness?
Like an unfaithful wife, my mental state departs from you, abandoning the five objects of desire.
Moreover, for one attached to sense-objects, there is no attainment of liberation; what then shall I do, O Lord of Sages? Grant me your service!
O most beloved one, Supreme among Men, Foremost Buddha, remover of weariness, Siddha of world-renowned fame!
Be my refuge, O you who possess unsurpassed grace; at every step, I am the servant of your very servants.
O Ten-Powered One, I am weak in this age of strife, submerged in the high waves of the ocean of long-standing misdeeds;
how may I follow your ship of Dharma? O Jina, grant me the support of your compassionate hand!
Having seen the manifold sufferings of existence and being terrified by fear, I have offered this prostration to you many times.
O Jina, support me with the hand of your compassion as I fall, weighed down by an exceedingly heavy thirst.
O Jina, your compassion for the world is indeed impartial; by virtue of that, look upon me too, though I am corrupted by faults.
It is enough; may I become happy, for the moon does not move differently toward the virtuous and the non-virtuous, acting with equal rays.

O Friend of the Wretched, quickly [save] the person who is blind from the mass of accumulated great delusion, devoid of compassion, bereft of the scent of self or kin, stripped of virtue and knowledge, risen with sin, and lacking discernment.
Whatever heavy misdeeds I have committed in the past through my body, speech, and mind—may they all dissolve moment by moment through the recollection of your feet, O All-Knowing One. (BuSto 18.41)
O Sugata, O you of sweet wisdom, I have fallen upon the earth before you in a prostration like a staff;
by your power, may all my unwholesome deeds fall away and never rise again, along with this very act.
I worship only your lotus-feet; I honor only your lotus-feet;
I meditate upon only your pair of feet; your state alone is forever my deity.
I speak not to anyone, I honor no one, I praise no one, I think of no one, nor do I feel affection for anyone;
I go to no one for refuge, having abandoned all but your feet, O Father, I am your servant.
In every assembly, in every word, on every path, on every road, in every house,
in every dwelling— here, on every earth, in every drop of water, may my mind always perceive this Lord of the World.
I gaze upon the Buddha incessantly with a mind free from passion, as if with my very eyes;
yet when I lie down at night placing you within my heart, those very moments are no different for me from being apart from you.
For me, a day here would indeed be a "bad day" (durdina) [if it were] covered by dark clouds; but that is not a bad day for me.
May that day never be mine which is devoid of the mindfulness of the name of the Jewel-Buddha, who is like nectar.

Those people who day after day recite the names "Giver of Immortality," "Possessor of the Six Superknowledges," "King of Dharma," "One Venerated by the Three Worlds," "Lord of Sages," and "Gautama"—even if they are not my devotees, I bow to those fortunate ones. (BuSto 18.48)
“O Daśabala, Jina, Siddha, Vajrabuddhi, Sugata, Tathāgata, Buddha, Śākyasiṃha!”—whosoever utters this at any time or place, even if born of a lineage of slaves, him I bow down to. (BuSto 18.49)
O Conqueror of Māra, O Victorious One, O Teacher, O Lord, O Leader, O Most Excellent Knower of the Universe;
O Best of Poets, O Sovereign of Speakers, O Son of Śuddhodana, O Śākyamuni, O Sage, be gracious!

O Lord of Men, even after drinking nectar, they must once again suckle at the teat of a bitch; but one who has tasted even once the essence of the nectar of your speech never again enters a mother's womb.
O Blessed One, I am unable here to endure the afflictions of birth, old age, death, and the like;
have compassion for me, for I know not where to go, having considered that heavy suffering among animals and other realms.

Reflecting further upon this, O Jina, my mind trembles helplessly at the thought of being rendered powerless over my hands, feet, eyes, and other faculties in old age; what shall I do, O Lord? Be gracious!
Since I direct my thirst even toward an object never seen before that produces happiness as soon as it enters the path of hearing,
therefore my mind turns toward and delights in you, the seed of peace, incessantly.
Therefore, my mind does not delight in the happiness of gods and men that has been enjoyed again and again in the past,
for one who has perceived its faults loses interest even in sugar candy after tasting it day after day.
The fool disregards, by his very gestures, the priceless wish-fulfilling gem already held in the palm of his hand;
how could I, having abandoned the jewel of the Buddha, be considered wealthy, virtuous, and wise in this world?
O Jina, he who possesses unwavering devotion toward you becomes wise, of noble birth, virtuous, renowned, and heroic; he is honored in the world and is truly happy. (BuSto 18.57)

O Victor, he by whom devotion to you is perfectly steadfast has studied everything here, has heard everything, and has practiced it all; he has conquered the entire universe, even though it remains unconquered by others.

Out of respect for one's own tradition, a person does not allow others to see their view; indeed, out of reverence for his mother, a child would surely not swallow a poisonous pill, even if it were life-threatening.
"O Jina, I am but a mediocre poet; how could I not abandon you, O Sage?
For right vision, acting as a companion to the rays of the sun, dispels the continuous stream of afflictions that has set in. (BuSto_18.60)
For a person who turns his back on the state of the Sugata, what is the use of asceticism, what is the use of fame, and what is the use of anything else?
For a person who turns his back on the state of the Sugata, what is the use of asceticism, what is the use of fame, and what is the use of anything else?
May those who have no devotion for the feet of the Sugata never even be born upon this earth;
for it has been declared here that for men who have committed offenses, the destination of hell is certain and not otherwise.

O Jina, may the mind of King Āsa— though he has mastered all the sciences, is born of a noble lineage, and possesses excellent form, youth, and so forth— abandon its impurity like that of a low-born man, for it does not attend upon you.
May even one of low birth, having cast off intoxication, pride, and envy, possessing compassion, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration,
and being discerning, become my friend in every life— a supreme man with firm devotion to your feet.
The life of a devotee who has performed the worship of the Victor’s feet for even ten days is praiseworthy;
it is not so for one who has performed worship of the lotus-feet of the Lord of Munis for millions of billions of kalpas.

He becomes a companion of the celestial beauties and rejoices in the worship performed by others; O Teacher of gods and men, he does so with devotion if, due to having no other recourse, he is unable to perform your own worship.

O Lord of Poets, that noble person who brings your image— so beautiful, exceedingly variegated, and of wondrous form— before the path of his eyes, abandons even those long-accumulated misdeeds, O Master.
He who bows before an image of those two made of jewels, gold, stone, or other materials,
and he who bows before you, O Jina, standing right in front of you— both obtain an equal fruit here, through the uninterrupted clarity of their minds.

The wise person who performs even a single act of worship at your lotus feet with forest flowers attains that stainless sovereignty which is radiant with the garlands from the crowns of the hosts of gods bowing down before it.

O holy Samantabhadra, refuge of the multitude, if the mass of merit arising from taking refuge for even a single moment of mind were to become equal [to that of all beings], it would then exceed the entirety of space.
O Sage, your virtues enter into that person who is pleased by the recounting of your qualities;
just as when the moon rises, the frost from the stream of its rays enters the moonstone.

O Sugata, even that which was offered but once by people who have abandoned delight in existence has, like the blade of your sword, severed all the faults such as the outflows, just as a sharp edge cuts down a tree. (BuSto 18.72)
Whatever good deed is performed here with a false view indeed results in its own bitter ripening;
just as a sown seed of the neem tree turns the essence of earth and water into its own bitterness.
Having fallen at your lotus-like feet, one never again falls into the four miserable realms;
for no person who performs wholesome deeds ever goes to an evil destiny anywhere, O Protector.
Having understood this through your instruction, I am devoted to the worship of your lotus feet.
May the Blessed One, casting away my poor intellect in birth after birth, establish in me noble devotion in age after age.

O Blessed One, even though my hands, feet, eyes, and other senses are steady for a moment at your words, the host of enemies violently agitates my heart; O Lordless One, protect, protect this helpless one!
If one strives to bring the eye under control, then the ear runs away;
and after that, alas, the tongue, nose, and body are likewise mutually difficult to restrain.
The course of the mind, which is exceedingly fickle, may here proceed without obstruction like the wind in the sky;
yet, through the practice of long-term detachment, it gradually attains a certain degree of steadfastness.
Though my mind is clear by nature, it may have been rendered dark by the long-accumulated stains of evil;
how then can it be washed clean by those drops of the water of virtue acquired by me with such a state of mind?

O supreme among men, with the streams of the nectar of your most pure words, instantly purify me—whose mental continuum has been defiled by passion and who am intensely tormented by suffering; I bow down to you like a staff.
O Sage, the teacher of all, when you are pleased, what is difficult to attain here or what is difficult to attain there?
For your servants, whose minds are stainless, do not value even the sovereignty of the Lord of the Gods in their thoughts.
The sense faculties produce fear in abundance when grasping at objects as if they were poison, due to the perception of their defects;
for even a child who has well-recognized the danger of being burned would not seize the tip of a lamp’s flame.
O Victor, as long as this [body] has not yet decayed through indulgence in the demons of sensory objects,
quickly employ me— who have come to you for refuge— in well-performed deeds, O you who are compassionate toward those who seek shelter!
Even if I know this— sons, wife, my own body, house, and so forth— to be equal to water in a mirage,
yet if the notions of "mine" and "I" still shroud me, that too is indeed the profound manifestation of delusion.
Everything is born from its own cause, and it is discarded, decays, and perishes by its own cause.
For I too am likewise a mere heap of elements; O Sage, how can I belong to this, and how can this belong to me?
In this world, for whomsoever the notion of a self arises, that notion will produce in them the sense of "I.
That sense greatly expands their craving for existence; it is that very thing which repeatedly generates delusion.
By means of that [self], one performs actions, both auspicious and inauspicious; for those indeed give rise to suffering within the three realms.
Therefore, the notion of a self is the very root of suffering; O Conqueror, cut it away with the sword of my words.
Now I praise the Lord, the knower of all, the ocean of compassion, the cause of the causes of the three worlds,
the noble one, who has gone everywhere, the infinite, the peace that exists, and the swan in the minds of sages.
O Lord, during bathing, ritual acts, eating, giving, smelling, as well as hearing,
meditating, touching, seeing, and likewise in conversation and so forth—
in the morning, in the evening, by day, and by night— [my mind remains] in Your lotus feet.
O Lord of Sages, may my mind always take delight in you, as the hearts of young men delight in a young woman.

O my Master, O wish-fulfilling tree for my desires, O my Deity, O my Guru, O my Mother, O my object of worship, O my dear friend, O my true refuge, O my Father, O my Knowledge, O pacifier of all my suffering, O my meditation, O my Abode!
O you who are liberated by me, O you of my noble fortune, O you who are my life-breath, O you who are my Buddha, protect me!
O Sugata, in praising you, Brahmā became downcast; the Guru lost his gravity; the Sun, the leader of the day, became leaderless;

Viṣṇu fell into thirst; the Sage ceased to be a sage; and even Īśvara became non-Īśvara. Śeṣa, whose power is the support of all, found his speech regarding Indra shattered in the face of your praise.
O Lord of gods and men, who am I—a foolish and wretched being—to proclaim your virtues?
The body of that meritorious one, upon which the marks of a Great Man shine brilliantly with eighty secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana) flashing forth from twenty-one times ten,
does not equal even a sixteenth part of his [the Buddha's] splendor.
The host of gods has four faces; what need is there to mention [the stature of] men?
Like the fresh rainbow of Mahendra upon the Golden Mountain, a captivating circle of brilliant light always flashes forth on every side;
for whosoever here has it within the range of their vision, let them hasten.
It removes that unsurpassed darkness far away, both within and without.
Your form captivates the eyes; your speech bestows a flood of bliss upon the ears; your compassionate influence utterly deludes the world;
and your tranquility is supreme, O Blessed One, whose very name is "the Omniscient," for your wisdom is renowned throughout the worlds.
And the renunciation of imperial power in his youth was clearly the ultimate limit of dispassion.

The gods have acknowledged your heroism in that you crush the pride of those with uneven arrows; for by your shafts, this world—including its gods, asuras, and Yama—was conquered, O wielder of the discus.
Your valor was made manifest most clearly by your direct realization of nirvāṇa.
How can we describe the power and majesty of the Blessed One, by which this world was made difficult to bear?
Since you even condemn in the Veda the ritual for slaughtering goats and horses, you are compassionate toward living beings; therefore, there is no one greater than you in mercy.
Thus, these perfections of your virtues are not within the scope of the intellect of those whose nature is envious.
Those fools prattle on, "Alas! This Sugata is a reviler of my doctrine."

May that fortune of your noble fame— which is the kinswoman of the foam on the Mandākinī as it flows from the breasts of the celestial beauties plunging therein, and which is a friend to the white lotuses of the Ocean of Milk—
not now embrace me, unfortunate as I am; yet, let it not fail to do so even for this much longer.
O Blessed One, physician for attachment, illness, and the like, this too is my prayer.
Those virtuous ones who go to you, the Buddha, for refuge do not go to an evil destiny;
having abandoned their human bodies, they then obtain divine bodies of unsurpassed happiness. [They are freed from] bad dreams, ill omens, malevolent serpents, harmful planets, and wicked beings.
Even painful diseases do not sometimes approach those who are virtuous in this world in such a manner.

Brahmā held a spotless parasol made of jewels for him, the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) held a fly-whisk, and the sages, Hara, and the serpents were his panegyrists with prose and verse; Mahendra was the vendor of conch-shells,
while others stood with lamps, water-pots, banners, and flowers shining in their hands, bowed down in devotion.
O Lord of Sages, having descended to earth from heaven, they remained there expounding the Dharma.
He for whom another's wife is like a mother, who has no longing for another's wealth, who does not speak falsely, who does not drink intoxicants, who does not kill living beings,
who fears the breaking of moral boundaries, whose heart is compassionate, and who has abandoned all pride— [he is a true man].
O Blessed One, he alone, being righteous in nature, is capable of performing the worship of your feet.
In this world, he who has desisted from all killing of living beings, from seizing the wealth of others, from sexual union with women, from false speech, and from intoxicants;
and from singing, garlands, perfumes, ornaments, dalliance, and high beds and seats— [he attains the first dhyāna].
O Teacher of gods and men, was that very wise one indeed your son? There is no doubt in this matter.
The paths of stream-entry and so forth, endowed with their six constituent parts, destroy the defects of passion and the like;
those defects, with their roots severed and their rebirths destroyed, attain peace along with their fruits.
For the new [paths], the abandonment of afflictions is the cause of the eternal, deathless, and undecaying state.
The cause of these phenomena is your word, O Jina; and the cause of that [word] is you alone.
Having shattered the twenty mountains of the view of a self-identity with the vajra of stainless wisdom,
they uproot all karma arising from the extremes of passion, hatred, and other evils; thus,
there are four who have attained the path, and likewise four who possess the fruits corresponding to that path.
Therefore, O Lord of Munis, we do not further consider the Noble Saṅgha to be distinct from you.
Even as space is infinite, so too are all sentient beings infinite;
this entire vast Cakravāla is infinite. O Jina, you speak thus having realized it through the infinite range of your wisdom.
And you, O Buddha, likewise know your own infinite qualities.
May devotion toward the Blessed One— the infallible destroyer of worldly existence— arise in me birth after birth;
may the Dharma be my instructor in every way.
Let it be so, let it be so; the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit.
By whatever pure and abundant merit has been acquired here through praising you, the Buddha, who are worthy of honor in the three worlds,
may all sentient beings in the world attain the awakening of a Perfectly Enlightened One.
May they, having shaken off various evils through meditative cultivations, proceed [to liberation].
While the illustrious Parākramabāhu, the lord of Laṅkā, the sovereign of kings, the sun to the lotus-clan of the radiant solar dynasty,
was ruling the earth with wisdom; there lived the wise Śrī Rāmacandra, a true Gauda and a divine sage among poets, who was like a god on earth to Bhāravi.
He composed the *Śrītṛṇa-bhaktiśataka*, which bestows dharma, wealth, and liberation.

The *Bhaktiśataka*, composed by the supreme lay devotee of the Blessed One, the Lord Śākyamuni, the Omniscient One— the Mahāpaṇḍita Ācārya Bhūsura, the sovereign of the glorious Buddhist scriptures from the land of Gauḍa— is hereby completed.
The king, whose arms possessed supreme valor, the crest-jewel among rulers of the earth and the friend of the circle of scholars,
made Rāmacandra— the twice-born son of the poet Bhārati— the sovereign of the Buddhist scriptures.

May the Buddha, the Victorious One, be my conqueror; may the teaching of that Blessed One remain stainless; may it shine for the benefit of sentient beings; and may the Saṅgha, its support, be proclaimed. May the kings, headed by the Lord of Laṅkā, always protect the earth with diligence.
May the thunderclouds rain at the proper time, and may all living beings attain loving-kindness.
The disciple of the venerable Lord Rāhula— who was the lord of the village of Tīrtha, a master of the Tripitaka, a preceptor of the royal lineage,
and the supreme lord of sages— was the wise sage Sumaṅgala, who [composed this] in his own language.
Out of compassion, he delivered an exposition of the *Munīndrabhaktiśataka*.
Homage to the Buddha, the Teacher; homage to the Dharma, the instruction;
homage to the great Saṅgha—homage always to these three as well.
Success!
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 19:
*Buddhabhaṭṭārakastotram* (Hymn to the Lord Buddha)
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
I pay homage to the perfectly awakened one, the lotus-eyed, the omniscient, whose nature is compassion, the teacher Samantabhadra, the Lion of the Śākyas. BuSto_19.1 //

I bow down to Śrīghana, the glorious one, the most excellent, the mass of coolness, the bringer of auspiciousness, the illustrious one, the maker of fortune, the peaceful one, and the one whose form is peace.
I bow to Indu, the proponent of selflessness, who is faultless, without support, learned in the scriptures, pure in nature, and free from grossness.

I bow to the Tathāgata, who brings about cessation, whose wisdom is eternal, who is free from conceptual construction, who is certain, whose hair is not disheveled, and who is beyond all proliferation.
I bow to Viśveśvara, the knower of liberation, the universal-formed Vināyaka,
the perfectly accomplished Viśvabrahma who is free from passion.
I bow to the Lord of the Universe, who is endowed with knowledge and conduct, whose radiance is stainless, who is free from sinking [in saṃsāra], possessed of steadfastness, and devoid of delusion.
I bow down to the Sage, the son of Śuddhodana, who tames the untamable, who is peaceful and pure, the Sugata, the one of auspicious rebirth, the gentle one of radiant fame.
I bow to the Lord of Yoga, the One of Ten Powers, the Knower of the World, the One Honored by the World,
the Teacher of the World, the Embodiment of the World, and the Protector of the World.
I bow to him who is the embodiment of gold, who is stainless amidst the ocean of karma, who possesses all the arts, whose form is lovely, who is a vessel of compassion, and who has a golden luster.
I bow down to him of great intelligence, great heroism, great wisdom, and great power; to him of great majesty, great fortitude, and mighty arms.
I pay homage to Amitābha, the primordial purifier, that Brahma, the unconquered and marvelous, the noble one who benefits others, the Protector.
I bow down to the God of gods, the Great God, the divine, the one who is worshipped, the imperishable,
the authoritative Lord of gods, who possesses a divine form.
I bow to the Blessed One, the ultimate reality, the supreme light, the highest Lord, the most excellent creator of both existence and non-existence.
I bow to Śiva, the benefactor, who has conquered the four Māras and the like, who knows reality, who is the essence of reality, whose conduct is always virtuous, and who is the caravan leader.
I bow down to the Lord of Jinas, the Supreme among Men, who has conquered the senses and conquered the afflictions; the highest, the true state, the Brahman, the field of merit.
Having praised the best of sages with these [verses], men, freed from all taints,
attain the divine and eternal state of liberation.
The wise person who, having risen early in the morning, constantly recites this hundred and eight pure names that destroy all evil, [attains the highest goal].
One obtains desired enjoyments described as being accompanied by mental ease;
even diseases do not afflict one, and one's transgressions are destroyed.
Endowed with long life, health, sovereignty, and complete liberation,
he is born intelligent and eloquent in birth after birth.
The hymn to the Lord Buddha composed by Brahmā is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 20:
Buddhagaṇḍīstavaḥ (The Praise of the Buddha’s Ghaṇṭā)
By the Master Aśvaghoṣa:
He who, formerly at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the path of the sun, [subdued] the Māras with incessant mantras of soft and harsh dual sounds— *gaṃgau gaṃgau gagaṃgau ghaghanaghana*.
May the Lion of the Śākyas, who was not moved to agitation by women of divine form with their exceedingly beautiful voices, and who is honored by gods and men, protect you.
He who [is known] by the "ka-ka-ha-ka-ha-ha" laughter of the women of Kandarpa; by the "ha-ha-ha" shouts and the "taṭi-taṭa-taṭa-tāṭa-tī" clamors of those with vast pomp;
and by the words of the servants—*kut-kut*, *budbuda*, *kukūcit*, and *kukuhakuhakuhaiḥ*.
May that Lord of Sages—gentle, whose every stain has been washed away by learning, and who is free from all fear—be for your peace.
By the casting of eyebrows and the contraction of the outer corners of the eyes; by the glances of eyes whose lashes and pupils shimmer like the arrows of Smara;
by the graceful movements of limbs that act as a dance performed by the tender vine-like arms of women mature in passion;
and by bashful, smiling words—utterances charming with their soft, sweet, and fragrant resonance—[the hearts of the young men were captivated].
Homage be to him, by whom even the mind’s delusion was not surprising, for he has conquered the power of Smara.
Shaking the broad earth, covering the sky with volleys of sharp arrows,
setting the ten directions ablaze with the flames of their wrathful fire, and agitating the ocean;
the heroic Māras roared with the sharp sounds of swords, discs, and saws brandished with ease.
May that Lord of Sages protect you, by whom [the enemies] were forcibly conquered with the weapon of loving-kindness.
Terrible with the roar of a manifest, formidable display of wrath thundering forth;
creating darkness with the massed pride of herds of elephants revealed by clouds of thundering rain;
illuminating the entire universe with the rays of his flashing sword, like the fierce fire of the God of Love.
May that Buddha protect you, by whom the lofty army of the Flower-Arrowed One was instantly shattered.

With the eyes of the women of Māra— filled with divine collyrium, resembling lotus petals, long-lashed, with trembling pupils, tender with emotion, clever, moving gracefully, accompanied by smiles and the play of the eyebrows,
encircled by earrings, with red corners, and restless— [the world was overwhelmed].
I bow to that best of sages, who has vomited out all faults and is in no way drawn [by worldly things].
His mind was not bewildered by Māras— those with clearly visible, formidable manes, with flickering tongues, holding tridents in their hands, with faces like elephants and horses,
and mouths like lions and tigers— by whom even Pradyumna, the god of love, who fears agitation, was disregarded as if he were a blade of grass.
May the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Sovereign of Sages, who is free from all defilement, protect you.

He whose intellect is unshakeable— even by the infinite, roaring Māra-soldiers of terrible form with hundreds of diverse faces, who are like the waters of the earth, mountains, rivers, oceans, and clouds;
he by whom that Puṣpaketu was disregarded like a blade of grass— he is the All-Knowing One, free from passion.
May that glorious Hero among Buddhas, the remover of the fear of defilement and free from passion, protect you.

The mind of him whose firm cross-legged posture remained unshaken— immovable like a mountain— even by the most fierce hosts of Māra’s daughters with swords, axes, bows, spears, and tridents in their hands, and by many falling meteors, deep and piercing sounds, and terrifying, formidable roars; [He] who was not agitated, his mind as steady as a mountain, while maintaining a firm paryanka-bandha.
I pay homage to that hero among Buddhas, the preeminent hero, who is worthy of veneration and who removes the fear of the three realms of existence.

Even by his servants— those hollow-eyed ones with matted locks thickened by the forceful slapping of their hands in arrogant sport, ringing bells fastened to their manifest and skillful warriors, and laughing with loud,
piercing shouts— they were unable to break his awakening through the beating of sharp drums and cymbals.
May that Heroic Buddha, who was as skillful as a sharp drum upon Gṛdhrakūṭa for those who were arrogant, be for your benefit.
Kokaṇḍa, Rāmakaṇḍa, Pratibhayakuhara, Darpadarpa, Raṇāṇḍa, Ḍimba, Ḍimba, Ḍaḍimba, Ḍuha, Ḍuhaka, Ḍuha, Tṛṃkhala,
Tṛṃkhala, Tṛm, Jhimba, Jhimba, Jhajhimba, Khamu, Khamu, Khamukha, Maṃkhu, Maṃkhu, Khumaṃkhu.
Unafraid by these sounds, the Lion of the Śākyas, saluted by the best of gods, may he protect you!

At night, the splendor of perfect enlightenment— whose sole partisan was opposed to the beauty of the lotus-forest-like faces of the daughters of Māra, who were intent on the frantic onset of their pact bearing the coals of Māra— attained him, just as the autumnal moonlight reaches the moon.
This is the gong of the Blessed One, the King of Dharma; it resounds as his messenger of the Dharma.

Since Death, whose end is never reached, slays even for a moment after a long time, you who have cast your minds upon that which is difficult to overcome must at all times show devotion to virtuous deeds.
Thus does he speak repeatedly to living beings, as if issuing the command of the Three Jewels— this is that [Dharma].
This is the gong of the Dharma, resounding so that its fame fills the circle of the quarters with its resonant voice.
Having conquered the host of heretics as the orb of the sun outshines the multitude of stars, the Jina’s teaching shines here;
the Gaṇḍī of Yama, the ornament of the earth’s surface, resounds joyfully like the fierce drum of victory.
That which possesses extreme firmness— *jami jami*, *ḍuḍubhaṃ*, *rañjitena alināliṃ*, *ḍimbaṃ ḍimbaṃ*, *ḍiḍimbaṃ*, *ḍubhaḍubhaḍuḍubhaṃ*,
*nāḍivan nāḍibhaṇḍam*, *ruṇḍaṃ ruṇḍaṃ*, *ruruṇḍaṃ*, *yaralava*, *khakhumaṃ*, *maṃkhumaṃkhuḥ*, *khumaṃkhuḥ*.
Behold, in this world of living beings, the army of Māra is being oppressed by the One who possesses the power of the ten strengths.
The king of mountains, Meru, trembles as the earth shakes from the upheaval of an earthquake; the hosts of gods, together with the multitudes of planets and all the kings of the nāgas,
are terrified upon hearing the fierce ghaṇṭā, which causes manifold fears and strikes terror into the heretics.
For the sake of peace for the Buddhists, it immediately resounds, making the earth ring out as if crying aloud.
This gong resounds upon the peak of the monastery and produces delightful sounds with the voice of a thundercloud;
like a mother out of affection, the meal-time gong calls to her sons who have gone far away.

The Gaṇḍī bell, whose sound is like the drum of the gods, resounds for the Buddha— who is intent on turning the wheel of saṃsāra and who is adorned with the jewels of all virtues— warding off all misfortunes.
For this gong resounds to awaken men, gods, humans, and asuras.
O noble ones, listen to the gong of the Sugata, which is being struck by the entire assembly of monks.

Where, even today, do people— trembling with fear at the suspicion of its destruction— scatter through the sky like clouds agitated at the time of universal dissolution by the *nāgas*, in order to counteract it;
[that place] whose sound still suppresses the pride of all rival sectarians?
May that gong, established by all the supreme sages for the increase of the Dharma, protect you all.
This gong of the Tathāgata— who is honored by gods, asuras, and great serpents, and who has attained supreme peace—
resounds with a voice like the drum of the immortals, rending the hearts of those of other sects.
"O people, be intent upon merit which bestows heaven and liberation;
do not commit sin, which brings about miserable rebirths. Life is fleeting! Thus, with effort, I have tried to restrain you from the humming of bees that has settled within me."
May this handful of flowers offered at the lotus feet of the Enemy of Māra protect you!

As he was descending from heaven to earth, Indra and the hosts of gods, led by Śakra, respectfully followed him for a long time, scattering flowers, filling the quarters with the sounds of musical instruments, and crying out "Jojoka! in jubilation.
May the fierce gong of that Blessed One, the ocean of compassion, protect the world.

Having taken seven steps immediately upon emerging from his mother’s womb, he, whose mind was focused on no other, himself uttered the words, "This is mine, the stream of saṃsāra. Furthermore, when he had been addressed as the Self-born One, the three worlds shone forth brilliantly.
May that Gaṇḍī of the Victorious Sugata shatter your darkness.
Having conquered the host of Māra, which causes great terror, and having brought about the destruction of all faults,
he attained that most beautiful state of omniscience right there on the night outside;
[I pay homage] to that Buddha, the wise one of pure self, who is a mine of all virtues without exception.
May the Gaṇḍī, which destroys fierce and fragmented sins, lead to the prosperity of men.
Brahmā became as if dejected; the Preceptor of the Gods completely cast off his pride; Śarva’s mind was humbled; and the Lord Viṣṇu remained silent.
Thus, when his virtues were being proclaimed, the gods fell into a state of mute silence out of shame.
May this gong of that Sage prevail for you, and may it protect the world from the lower realms.
Brahmā, Āditya, Śaśāṅka, Śaṅkara, Śatākṣa, Upendra, Yakṣas, and others; Gandharvas, Uragas, Kinnaras, Asuras, Samīras, Pretas, Pīḍās, and Ambaras—
those immortals who abide among men upon the surface of the earth and in the worlds of the nether regions (pātāla).
Let all of you come together to hear this Dharma from the Teacher, the Tathāgata.
At her birth, the non-Buddhist teachers, their minds base and inferior, were filled with grief;
while the Buddhists, their intellects nourished by an extraordinary height of joy, attained steadfastness.
Having encountered her, virtues expand to their full extent and faults come to an end.
May that *gaṇḍī*, which removes the defilements of the Kali age, be for your prosperity.
Having bowed according to the prescribed rite to that [Dharma-gong] of the Sage, those of pure intellect attain the lofty state;
and all adversaries, rendered powerless, go swiftly to their destruction.
That Dharma-gong of the Sage has shattered and scattered the entire veil of delusion.
May it arise together to dispel the fear of existence for you, long-lived ones.

Upon hearing it, Brahmā and the other gods fell to the surface of the earth; the inhabitants of heaven trembled, the mountains shook, and even the earth quickly sank into the depths of the underworld.
This [teaching], which causes fear among the heretics, was proclaimed by one whose soul was purified by the undertaking of the welfare of others.
Let that mallet be struck immediately for the sake of the Buddhists' pacification.
Mounted upon the mature [Gaurī] in the *ālīḍha* posture, with his heavy foot treading upon the tips of Gaurī’s breasts,
the All-Knowing One, whose upper body resounds with hundreds of clearly manifest and formidable roars,
his limbs blazing with a garland of flames, is terrifying with the *huṃkāra* that pervades the cavities of the three worlds.
Victorious is he whose crown is bound with both the bound and the unbound—the sun and moon among gods, humans, and lords of asuras.
With songs and musical instruments, the deer-eyed, amorous women— possessing full and lofty breasts and the graceful gait of swans—
produced rhythmic clapping sounds: *daṃ daṃ daṃ daṃ da daṃ daṃ*, *tani tani tanitaḥ*,
and *tuṃ tuṃ tuṃ tuṃ tatuṃ tuṃ* all around the waist-drum.
"Ṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭuṭuṃ ṭuṃ ṭumiti"—this ghaṇṭikā is struck with measured intervals. // BuSto_20.32 //
The *Buddhagaṇḍī* is completed.
This is the work of the venerable master Ācārya Śrī Aśvaghoṣa.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 21:
Buddhastotram (Praise of the Buddha)
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha! Homage be to the Buddha, whose awakening is utterly pure, whose awakening is the manifestation of the utterly pure Dharma,
whose subsequent awakening has approached the merit of the True Dharma, who is empty of the peak of existence, and whose awakening is utterly pure.
Aho! Aho! The Buddha of infinite splendor; aho! aho! the ocean, Meru, and the forest grove!
Aho! aho! the Buddha of infinite range, as exceedingly rare as the flower of the udumbara tree.
"Oh, how great is the Tathāgata of great compassion! Oh, oh, the banner of the Śākya clan!

The gong, through the resonance following the sequence of blows from its staff, vibrates like a great drum.

All have approached with humility at the soles of his feet; I praise him with songs of mantra.
Causing the ignorant to wander through the three worlds while leading those who possess the knowledge of all-knowing lords together with the state of the Sages;
terrifying all the Māras and other various types of beings who cause fear in many ways;
driving away all evils; and awakening the wise from their thoughts of delight in sense-objects.
The gong of the Lion of the Śākyas resounds loudly throughout the world for those whose awakening is obstructed.

To him who, having given his own body to a tigress, attained Buddhahood—acquired through a mass of merit and a multitude of hundreds of virtues; he who has warded off evil, seeks to intoxicate the god of love, is the peerless Teacher, and has shattered the fear of existence and the intent toward sin; [to him I bow].
This indeed is that wondrous gaṇḍī of the Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas, which resounds.

By Māras of various kinds— with swords, axes, bows,

and arrows in their hands; with blazing, terrifying faces, wicked fangs, and the faces of elephants, serpents, lions, and dogs— even for a single moment, they could not overcome the feet of that Buddha, who was bowed down by his adversaries.

I bow to the Lord of Obstacles— dwarfish yet exceedingly stout, with the face of a lordly elephant, pot-bellied and beautiful, his broad cheeks swarming with bees greedy for the scent of ichor;
who rends his enemies with the upraised stroke of his tusk and brings forth the splendor of vermilion.
I pay homage to Gaṇapati, the son of the Daughter of the Mountain, the bestower of supernatural attainments and the granter of desires.
Heramba is the supreme deity, the bestower of the accomplishment of all tasks;
grant me the abundance of happiness endowed with good fortune and beauty.
I bow to the son of Gaṅgā, who has a single tusk, a massive body, a protruding belly, and the face of an elephant; he is the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
I bow to that noble Gaṇanātha, the sinless one, who is a forest fire to the drought of poverty,
who shakes away all impurities with the trunk of his elephant's tusk, and who is a boat for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra;
by bowing to that supreme Lord, tens of millions of gods attain the highest perfection.
His body is crimson with vermilion, and he is drenched by streams of ichor flowing forth.
Bearing a pair of water-pots as lofty as the two halves of the cosmic egg,
delightful with his broad ears and palate that rival the wings of the enemy of the serpent’s foe (the peacock),
the Lord’s son, whose growing hands vie with the body of the lord of serpents—
Victorious is the elephant-faced Lord of the three worlds, whose form is a marvel to the three realms!
Gaṇapati, Heramba, Vidhṇarāja, and Vināyaka—
the son of the Goddess, possessed of great splendor, great strength, and great prowess.
Large-bellied and large-bodied, with a single tusk and the face of an elephant;
clad in white garments, greatly radiant, and three-eyed, he is the leader of the Gaṇas.
Holding a rosary and a tooth in his right hand,
and grasping an axe and a bowl of sweetmeats in his left hand.
The deity delights in various flowers, is anointed with various fragrances,
has a snake as his sacred thread, and is the destroyer of various kinds of obstacles.
I bow to him who is worshipped by gods, asuras, humans, siddhas, and gandharvas; the remover of obstacles for the three worlds, mounted upon a rat.
Sumukha, Ekadanta, Kapila, Gajakarṇaka, Lambodara,
Vikaṭa, Vināyaka, and the King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja).
Dhūmraketu, the leader of the Gaṇas, Bhālacandra, Gajānana, Vakratuṇḍa, Śūrpakarṇa, Heramba, and the elder brother of Skanda.
Whoever should recite or even hear these sixteen names at the commencement of learning, at a wedding, at entering [a house], or likewise at departing;
In battle and in times of distress, no obstacle arises for him.
Homage to the Lord of the Gaṇas, the axe for the creeping vine of obstacles.

*Guhyeśvarīstotram* (Hymn to Guhyeśvarī)
O Blessed One, who possesses manifold forms, who is changeless and untainted,
whose form is the cause of all forms and whose nature transcends all determination;
O You who stand at the further shore of all the Vedas, whose essential nature is both eternal and non-eternal.
O Goddess, I bow to your pair of lotus feet.
Your smiling moon-like face becomes the night through its radiance;
your face, with its hundred rays, becomes the midday sun; and at the time of sunset, the beauty of your reddened countenance becomes the rising dawn.
I bow to your pair of lotus feet, O Goddess.
In the regions of her throat and belly are the three worlds of heaven, earth, and the netherworld;
her rows of teeth are all the celestial bodies, and the lines of hair are trees.
Her hips are like mountains, and her red and white [garments] are the oceans.
O Goddess, I bow to your pair of lotus feet.
The winds and fires of your breaths, which possess the velocity of wind and fire, constitute both the time of dissolution and the time of creation through their closing and opening;
these twelve-fold rays of yours have become beings with terrifying faces.
O Goddess, I bow to your pair of lotus feet.
O Goddess, as your divine form— which is beyond all measure— pervades everywhere,
your intellect arises to reveal the entire three worlds, manifesting the essence of all the Vedas.
O Goddess, I bow to your pair of lotus feet.
Those gods who face the ritual procedure are your servants standing at your feet;
O pure one, all paths indeed rest upon the crown of your intellect.
O secret goddess, how can I possibly describe your majesty?
O Goddess, I bow to the pair of your lotus feet.
For one who, being devoted, recites this at the conclusion [of the ritual], during worship, or praises it with hymns, their intellect becomes clearly manifest; indeed,
their excellence of devotion toward the Mother of all beings increases greatly.
Placed in the palm of one's hand, they attain accomplishment and nourishment.
The Guhyeśvarī Stotra, composed by Mañjunātha and extracted from the Śrī Svayaṃbhū Purāṇa, is complete.

Oṃ! Homage to the Triple Gem!

[I prostrate] to that which has craving for its tongue, false conceptualization for its head, hatred for its quivering fruit, and which likewise displays desire, anger, and discursive thought, with passion as its fierce eye.
Homage to that Buddha who, by the power of the mantra of wisdom, has pacified the terrible mouth of delusion— which exceeds the thoughts of hundreds of millions of his own bodies.

I pay homage to that glorious Great Awakening—the Buddha, the fully awakened one, the sovereign of the sublime Dharma, the peaceful, the pure, the bestower of universal renown, the mine of virtues, the being who is the king of the lords of sages. BuSto_32.2 //
Thus ends the *Buddharatnastotra*.
He who is the eye for virtuous beings scorched by the heat of the sufferings of birth and so forth;
he who daily draws forth sentient beings from the cage of the triple world.

Homage to that Great Dharma which rescues the world, left without protection, from the ocean of afflictions and suffering, and which further delivers the perfectly awakened ones from the state of passing away.
That which, through omniscience, leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility;
that which, through the knowledge of the paths, accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of beings;
and that which is conjoined with all aspects of the universe—of this the Sages speak.
Homage to that Mother of the Buddha, who possesses a multitude of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
Thus ends the Hymn to the Jewel of the Dharma.
There are four who dwell in the present, who loathe the sweet taste of the pleasures of existence; and there are four who abide in the fruit, great yogis who delight in tranquility and are peaceful.
Homage to that Saṅgha, in which the Blessed One—whose body was refined by wisdom, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration—prophesied these eight excellent individuals. BuSto_32.5 //
I constantly bow to the Buddha, who holds the excellent lotus in his hand,
whose nature is loving-kindness, who is Gaganagañja and Samantabhadra,
the lord of yakṣas, who has cast off and uprooted Mañjughoṣa.
I bow with devotion to Viṣkambhin and Kṣitigarbha.
Thus ends the *Saṃgharatnastotra*.
The Buddha is the Guru, the Dharma is the Guru, and likewise the Saṃgha is the Guru;
the glorious Vajradhara is the Guru—to that glorious Guru, homage!
The *Śrī Gururatnatrayastotra* is completed.

Hāratīstotram (The Hymn to Hārītī)
Homage to the goddess Śrī Hārītī!

With devotion, I bow to the mistress of yakṣas who has many sons, whose body is like a jasmine flower, whose limbs are adorned with beautiful unguents, and whose adamantine body is decorated with various ornaments; she who, with her lotus-hand held to the right, dispels the fear of those afflicted by terror.
Her beautiful body was adorned with three eyes and embraced by her own right arm;
she wore a crown fashioned from various kinds of precious gems.
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, the mother of many sons.
She is situated within a mandala of fire, upon a lotus of eight petals and a precious jewel-throne; her lotus-feet rest above it,
she is surrounded by yakṣas and others, and she sits in the graceful posture (lalitāsana).
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, the mother of many sons.
To the one who pacifies the suffering of the three worlds, who bestows life upon children,
the illustrious Hārītī, who through her compassion is skillful toward her own devotees,
and who removes the misery of those possessing enchanting enjoyments—
I prostrate with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, who has many sons.
She who strikes terror into those of slanderous conduct, who destroys the mass of afflictions such as boils and other diseases,
who is like a mother to her devotees, and whose limbs are most cool.
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, who has many sons.
Delighting in the Buddha’s instruction, possessing an exceedingly subtle form,
her feet worshipped by the three worlds, she is the very radiance of compassion;
she is attended by hosts of gandharvas and kinnaras.
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, who has many sons.
Adorned with armlets, earrings, beautiful bracelets, and anklets, she was accustomed to wearing various and diverse garments;
she was one to be protected, as she was nurturing a group of children.
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, the mother of many sons.

Day after day, I remember her whose full heart is intent on bestowing enjoyment upon those dwelling in Svarga, Bhūḥ, and Rasātala, and who is the very embodiment of the three *guṇas*; I take refuge in her.
I bow with devotion to Yakṣeśvarī, who has many sons.
A person should recite this hymn to Śrī Hārītī, the protectress, within their own home for the protection of children;
[she bestows] speech, prosperity, and all vast happiness and the like.
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this triad at dawn, [is a giver].
The Hāratī Stotra, which emerged from the illustrious Bhavaraṇa and provides protection for children, is complete.

*Kalyāṇapañcaviṃśatistotram* (The Praise in Twenty-five Verses on Auspiciousness)
The glorious primordial self-arisen one, Amitābha of unerring name, the Buddha Akṣobhya;

the glorious one named Vairocana, the Lord of Munis born of jewels, Vajrasattva, the Great Being; the glorious Prajñā, the Vajradhātu who brings about all auspiciousness, and those such as Noble Tārā.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
The Goddess Sampatprasādā, Gaṇapatihṛdayā, Vajravidrāviṇī,
the Uṣṇīṣā Aparṇadevī, Kiṭivaravadanā, Mātṛkā of the Khecarīs, Koṭolalakṣākṣadeva, surrounded by her own hosts— the Five Protectresses (Pañcarakṣā), the excellent protection.

Among the Jewels are the one named Dīpaṅkara, the Victor Maṇikusuma, the glorious Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvambhu, the glorious Kakutsunda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyasiṃha;
and the present preeminent one, the possessor of all the ten powers, an ocean of supreme majesty.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow down to them.
The glorious Āryāvalokiteśvara, the supreme among the Conquerors; Maitreya, the infinite treasury; the Buddha Sāmantabhadra; Mañjunātha, the Great Lord who wields the excellent vajra;

May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
From the lotus born from the bulb of the Buddha’s empowerment, he named Nāgadāsa— who was the lord of youth— emanated a single light from his own excellent world;
having become fivefold as a single portion, he dwells eternally as the essence of the five Buddhas.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

May that Wisdom, whose form is secret, born from the three-petalled lotus, may Nairātmyā— whose nature is the sacred seat (pīṭha), who has accomplished manifold benefits, and who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa— be present through the grace of the gods; she who, having appeared in the unfathomable depths of Durgā when the entire path was being traversed, bestows the supreme boon upon those who bow before her.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
From a portion of Maitrīya arose Ratnacūḍa, whose crest-jewel was the great forest;
having attained the auspicious light, he became known as Ratnaliṅgeśvara, a vessel for the ocean of existence.
Śrīvatsa, whose greatness was established by the eight Vītarāgas, is the self-manifested one (Svayambhū) of manifest form.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
By the command of the Lord of the World, the son of the Jina named Khagañja became Padmākāra on the bank of the Vāgmatī city; he,
the illustrious Gokarṇeśvara, who destroyed his wicked father, recited [mantras] with a steady mind to save the corrupt Gokarṇa at this confluence of the Vāgmatī.

Frightening the enraged King of Nagas, who was like a Kulika serpent, like a stake for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, the Great Lord named Kali— who is free from passion— became the form of a banner atop the glorious mountain, moving as if in flight, bringing auspiciousness to the illustrious Sāmantas and others.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

To drink that [nectar] which has all its feet, Vajrapāṇi proceeds at the word of the Lotus-Bearer; for the sake of protecting the worlds, he has again become the form of a water-pot from a portion [of that nectar].

May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
Having made the difficult-to-understand Mañjugartavyajana— who delighted in pleasure— well-awakened through his beautiful wife, Mañjudeva thereafter made him a wise and great preeminent poet;
then, maintaining his breath and attaining the state of all virtues, he became known as Garteśa.
May they bring about your welfare whether you are moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

Where the Naga named Puṇya attained happiness from Tārkṣya at Anusukha;

May they bring about your welfare whether you are moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

For the poor who are devoted to worship, he is a treasure-trove; indeed, he is the sacred ford known as a mine for the wise, from whom knowledge is obtained by those of supreme intellect; he is the sole sacred ford named "Knowledge.

There, by those who bathed with joy, it became known as Āpti; and that Prāmodatīrtha bestowed excellent marks (*sallakṣaṇa*).
That which is called Tīrthasallakṣaṇa gave such marks to those moving within its own waters.
Having bathed there, the lord of the gods named Bala conquered the island named Ākhyambha-tīrtha.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
The goddess known as Vidyādharī, the sky-faring Yoginī preceded by Vajra, Hārīta, the illustrious Hanumān, along with Gaṇapati, Mahākāla, and the one named Cūḍā— these who are worthy of worship;
and the goddesses beginning with Brahmāṇī, together with Hari, Sukhavarakṣa, and Nāskanda.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

At the Vāgmatī, there are subsidiary pilgrimage sites (upatīrtha) such as Mūla and Puccha; likewise, the Keśacaityas, those situated on Śaṅkhocca, and that venerable Lord Caitya gracing Jātoccayagiri.
Then there are Phullocca, Draṣṭadevī, and the locations of Bhagavatī, Dhyāna, Procca, and others.
May they bring about your welfare whether you are moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
The stūpa named Mañjuśobha, fashioned by his attendants on Mount Mañjuśrī;
the natural abodes in the five divine cities created by Śāntaśrī;
and the supreme stūpa at the tip of the tail, where in the past at Śāketa he proclaimed the incomparable [teachings].
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

The one called Ādhāra resides in the heart; he is the lord of serpents with his attendants, the destroyer of the king of obstacles, and the Nāga in the lineage of the three worlds known as Hari, Hari-hari, and Harivāha in the world of Ānanda.
O Lord of the World, may you be capable [of protecting] us; thereafter, may the sole lord of the world fulfill our hopes and desires.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
Hevajra is that Saṃvara, together with his retinue and host; he is Caṇḍavīra, the hero of the three worlds, and Yogāmbara.
He is the ten Krodharājas, beginning with Yamāntaka, the destroyer of Yama.
All those who are secret and external, headed by Parimita—this is the explanation of the *Nāmasaṃgīti*.
May they bring about your welfare whether you are moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
On his head, accompanied by his retinue, that Moon-like King ascended the mountain of the Setting Sun;
having cut through the drying up of this lake, Mañjunātha— the lotus of the foremost city and the dwelling place of the world— remained in the restored waters and worshipped the Supreme Victor.
May they bring about your welfare whether you are moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.

From Sukhāvatī he went to Vaṅga, and thereafter, for the benefit of the people, he arrived at Potala; being peaceful when the fault of the crocodile arose, he entered the excellent city of Lalitapura, summoned by the gods.
He is the glorious Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the hosts of attendants such as Jaṭadhara and Hayagrīva.
May they bring you auspiciousness whether moving or staying anywhere; I bow to them.
The *Kalyāṇapañcaviṃśatistuti*, extracted from the *Śrī Svayambhūpurāṇa*, is completed.
