*Kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotra* (The Hymn in Thirty Verses on Auspiciousness)
Having entered into the state of the syllable *Evaṃ*, through body, speech, mind, and intellect,
I constantly perform praise, worship, and circumambulation of her.
To that Goddess who effects the creation and destruction of all sentient beings—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To the goddess who is established as the protector of all beings,
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who stands among the goddesses of gods in the form of a deity—to her, homage;
to her, homage; to her, homage; homage, homage!

To that Goddess who has a terrifying form for the purpose of burning the Daityas who are difficult to subdue—to her, salutations; to her, salutations; to her, salutations; salutations again and again!
To that goddess who is the thousand-faced queen of all nāgas— homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who dwells in the seven netherworlds in a peaceful form—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who is the Mother of the Vedas for men and women, the Consciousness-Mother (Cidambikā),
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, salutations again and again!
To that Goddess who is worshipped by the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who possesses great supernatural power for the protection of the realms of the departed,
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who delivers all animals and destroys their suffering—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
Homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again— to that Goddess who is the mother of those in hell and of all who partake in suffering.
To that Goddess who is the destroyer of the sixteen hells,
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage!
To that Goddess who has been made formidable by those possessed of hatred and passion, and by the deluded—to her, salutation!
To her, salutation! To her, salutation! Salutation, salutation!
To that Goddess who, through desire and anger, abides in the form of wrath—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who has tarried in order to leap over greed and gain—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage!
To that goddess who is the mother of Māyā, the Vajrayoginī of all mothers—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who destroys kings, thieves, fire, lions, and enemies— homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To the goddess who delivers one from the fears of water, serpents, nāgas, and famine— homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that Goddess who is established in the five elements, in the moon, and in the sun—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who is the temporal limit of the elements, who moves within the vowels and consonants—to her, homage;
to her, homage; to her, homage; homage, homage!
To that Goddess who is the sovereign of all sacred seats (pīṭha), the secondary goddess (upachandikā) in the form of the field (kṣetra),
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To the goddess who is called Pīlava and joined with Upapīlava—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage, homage!
To that Goddess who, adorned with the zodiac signs and the ascendant, resides in the twelfth wheel—
to her be homage, to her be homage, to her be homage, homage again and again!
To that Goddess whose moon-like face is fully awakened in the region of the six limbs—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her; homage, homage!
Salutation to that Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign who moves within the fierce wheels; salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation to her, salutation again and again!
To that Goddess who proceeds in the form of mantra within body, speech, and mind—
homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage again and again!
To that goddess who is pure in essence, the bestower of glory, prosperity, accomplishment, and strength—to her, homage;
to her, homage; to her, homage; homage, homage!
To that goddess who always brings auspiciousness to all living beings—homage to her, homage to her, homage to her; homage, homage!
The wise person who, endowed with devotion to the Goddess, recites this,
swiftly attains Buddhahood— auspicious, auspicious, and blissful.
The *Kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotra*, a hymn of praise in thirty verses to the Vajradevī who dwells within the three glorious bodies, is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 36:
*Kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotram* (The Hymn to All Tathāgatas by Kamalākara)
Then, indeed, in the Lotus Grove, with a hymn of praise to all the Tathāgatas, he offered supreme praise to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present—
those who were Jinas in former bodies and those who currently abide in the worlds of the ten directions.
I indeed pay homage to those Victors, and I shall take refuge in that assembly of Victors.
The Lord of Munis, peaceful, profoundly tranquil, and pure, whose body is radiant with the luster of finest gold,
whose voice possesses the exquisite resonance of all gods and asuras, and who thunders with the sound of the voice of Brahmā.
His hair is like a tree frequented by bees and the bumblebee, resembling the dark and beautifully curled kāśa flower;
his teeth are as white as a conch shell or snow, and the luster of his speech shines like gold.
With large, pure, and beautiful blue eyes like a field of blooming blue lotuses,
and with a lovely tongue radiant as gold from a lotus, he possesses the auspicious luster of words spoken from a lotus.
His navel was like a conch shell or a lotus stalk, a pleasant expanse with hair curling to the right;
it was like the subtle moon when it has waned, or like the beautiful lotus of Mātra and Sumantra.
I constantly pay homage to that Gentle-Handed One, the Victor of all, whose nose is as high as a well-crafted golden balance-beam and possesses very soft leaf-like nostrils,
and whose tip of the nose is distinguished by the excellence of the foremost among the foremost.
Each single hair on his face tips upward, while his fine body hairs curl to the right;
his beautiful neck is adorned with a crown of dark-blue, radiant earrings that shine with a deep azure luster.
His body possesses a radiance equal to that of the sun, honored throughout all the ten directions of the world;
he has pacified infinite suffering for the world and has satisfied the world with every form of happiness.
In those dwelling in hell, in the animal realms, and in the worlds of hungry ghosts, gods, asuras, and humans—
may all beings be granted happiness by the Piśācas, and may all states of miserable rebirth be completely stilled.
His complexion was like fine gold, with a luster resembling refined gold; his body was radiant with the glow of heated gold.
His face was as pure as the gentle moon, and his countenance was as beautiful and stainless as a full-blown lotus.
His body was as tender as the tips of young sprouts; he possessed the roar and prowess of a lion in combat;
his arms were long with hands hanging down; and his tongue was like the leaf of a *sāla* tree stirred by the wind.
The Lord of Sages, with his stainless and excellent body, blazing like the sun that emits rays from its celestial radiance, shines with splendor and illumines the entire infinite realm.
In infinite thousands of fields, they became like a mass of moons, stars, and suns;
and all of them became definitively established for the sake of radiating the splendor of a Buddha’s light.
May they behold the Buddha-sun, the lamp illuminating the world, with its thousands of rays of the Buddha-sun,
as the Tathāgata-sun appearing in worlds throughout infinite thousands of realms.
Having performed hundreds and thousands of meritorious deeds, his body was adorned with every excellence;
he resembled the lordly elephant of the sun, possessed of conquered arms, and his arms were decorated and protected by stainless [ornaments].
The Buddhas who have come are like the surface of the earth, equal to the expanse of rice fields, and like subtle dust;
those who exist are like subtle dust, and those who remain are like subtle dust.
With a clear mind, I offer salutations to those Victors with body, speech, and mind;
I remember them with purity through the offering of flowers, the offering of fragrances, and with hundreds of pure verses of praise.

Even with hundreds of tongues, it would take hundreds of thousands of eons to describe the qualities of the Buddhas, those well-liberated and sublime Victors; yet that [wisdom] is displayed upon the forehead in manifold and wondrous ways.
It is not possible to describe even a fraction of the qualities of a single Jina, even with a thousand tongues;
for it is impossible for all the Jinas together to speak in detail of even a single quality.
The entire multitude of all the worlds, including the realm of gods, and all the oceans of existence filled to the very peak of becoming—
even if one were able to grasp the measure of those waters, it would not equal even a single quality of the Sugata.
By this praise and excellent hymn to the entirety of the Jina’s body and speech,
may the supreme fruit of the accumulated merit be such that all sentient beings may attain the state of a Victor.
Indeed, O King, I make this vow that the entire world may be awakened by the Buddhas;
and wherever any birth might occur for me throughout infinite future eons.
In my dream I see such a drum, and there I hear such a sound;
may I obtain such praise of the Jina from Kamalākara there, remembering my births and old age.
The qualities of the Buddha are infinite and incomparable, and even those which are difficult to encounter in a thousand eons—
even those heard in a dream— he teaches them while he is awake during the day.
May I liberate sentient beings from the ocean of suffering and fulfill them with the six perfections;
may I attain unsurpassed awakening and merit, and may the light of the sun and moon illuminate this realm.
By the ripening fruit of the gift of the drum and for the sake of praising all the Victors, I behold the Lord Śākyamuni face to face; indeed, may I receive a prophecy there.
May I obtain there these two boys, my sons Kanakendra and Kanakaprabhāśvara,
and may both boys receive the prophecy of unsurpassed awakening.
And whatever beings there may be— countless and infinite, destitute of refuge, fallen into calamity—
in all those places may I, in the future, be their protector, their ultimate resort, and the giver of refuge.

O Lord, may I practice for the sake of awakening throughout future eons— both those yet to come and those that have passed since the beginningless past— acting as the one who brings about the destruction of the arising of suffering and as a mine of all happiness.
By the teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, may my ocean of evil be dried up;
may my ocean of karma be scattered, and may my ocean of afflictions be severed.
May my ocean of merit be filled, and may my ocean of wisdom be purified;
through the supreme radiance of stainless wisdom, may there be light for me according to my desire.
May I possess eyes of radiant merit and become preeminent throughout the entire three worlds;
may I be eternally endowed with supreme merit and be a deliverer from the ocean of suffering.
And for an ocean-like eon into the future, may I practice for the sake of all happiness;
through diligent effort, may I reach the limit of the past in such a distinguished realm as this within the three worlds.
The *Kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotra*, spoken by the illustrious Suvarṇaprabha, is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 37:
*Lokanāthastotram* (Hymn to the Lord of the World)
At the beginning of the aeon, who indeed was my origin? O you who are the essence of all, the embodiment of compassion, whose form is the universe!
At the beginning of all activity, I bow to you, the All-pervading One; O Śrī Lokanātha, I prostrate at your pair of feet.
O gentle Śrīlokanātha, returning daily with a dust that is not blackened, you come complete in every part upon a brilliantly shining chariot of golden form; I bow at your pair of feet.
You alone are indeed that Brahmā renowned in the community of Brahmins, and you are Viṣṇu in the Vaiṣṇava doctrine, the banner of supreme Dharma;
you are the Omniscient One, the source of all, and the imperishable—O Śrī Lokanātha, I bow at your pair of feet.
Within the lineage of the Buddha, you appear in the form of Vajrasūrya, the Lord of Yoga on the paths of auspicious yoga;
O Śrī Lokanātha, you who are like the bearer of the Gaṅgā and the destroyer of the fear of existence, I bow at your pair of feet.
With a heart whose nature is compassion, innate and radiant, you have severed the accumulation of defilements and are an ocean of virtues;
you are the wish-fulfilling jewel, the Teacher of the World, and the Lord of Mercy. O Śrī Lokanātha, I bow at your pair of feet.

O you of the color of the bandhūka flower, of many forms, with wide eyes, who have brought about the atonement for all births, O one with beautiful teeth! O Padmapāṇi, most pure and supreme, in the form of a friend, O Śrī Lokanātha, I bow to your pair of feet.
Who is capable of recounting your manifold deeds?
Nevertheless, I praise you here with eloquent expressions;
even if there be any impure word, please forgive all of this.
"Praise" refers to a garland of flowers; "worship" should consist of devotion alone.
The hymn to the venerable lord Śrīmad Āryāvalokiteśvara is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 38:
*Lokātītastavaḥ* (The Praise of Him Who Has Transcended the World)
Homage to you, who have transcended the world and perceive the knowledge of solitude;
you who, out of compassion, have long been weary for the very sake of the welfare of the world.
Since there is no sentient being existing apart from the mere aggregates, for that reason,
O Great Sage, you did not fall into weariness regarding the welfare of sentient beings.
O wise one, you have also fully revealed to the wise that those aggregates are like an illusion,
a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, and a dream.
How indeed could those things that arise from causes— not existing in the absence of those causes—
not be clearly understood as being like reflections?
Since the elements are not graspable by the eye, how can that which consists of them—the visual [object]—be so?
By speaking thus, you yourself have refuted the grasping of form.
Without that which is to be felt, there is no feeling; therefore, it is devoid of self. And you maintain that this object of feeling does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature.
If name and object were non-different, the mouth would be burned by fire;
if they were different, there would be no cognition—this was stated by you, the speaker of truth.
"You have stated that the agent is independent and so too is the action from the perspective of conventional usage;
however, the establishment of these two is intended by you to be mutually dependent."
"There is no agent, there is no enjoyer; merit and demerit are born dependently.
O Vācaspati, you have declared that whatever is dependently arisen is not truly born."
That which is not being made known cannot be an object of knowledge, nor can there be consciousness without it;
therefore, you have stated that both knowledge and the object of knowledge do not exist by way of intrinsic nature.
If the characteristic were other than the characterized, then that characterized would be without a characteristic;
you have clearly stated that both would be non-existent if they were not other.
This world has been seen by you with the eye of wisdom as peaceful, devoid of both the characterized and the characteristic, and free from the utterance of speech.
An existent entity does not arise, nor does a non-existent one, nor one that is both existent and non-existent;
it is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both—how then could it be born?
The destruction of an existent thing that is endowed with stability is not possible;
nor is it possible for a non-existent thing, which is equivalent to a horse's horn, to have any similarity [to existence]. How could there be equality?
Destruction is considered neither different from the entity nor non-different from it;
if it were different, it would be eternal, and if it were not different, it could not occur.
The destruction of an entity is not possible if it is identical [to itself];
for the destruction of an entity is only possible if it is distinct [from itself].
First of all, the arising of an effect from a cause that has already perished is not tenable;
nor is it tenable [for it to arise] from one that has not perished, for you consider its arising to be like a dream.
Whether from a seed that has ceased or one that has not ceased, the arising of the sprout occurs;
indeed, you state that all arising is like the manifestation of an illusion.
Therefore, you have fully understood that this world arises from conceptual construction; it is unreal, unarisen, and does not perish.
There is no cyclic existence for that which is eternal, nor is there cyclic existence for that which is impermanent;
O best among those who know reality, you have declared that cyclic existence is like a dream.
Logicians maintain that suffering is self-created, created by another, created by both, or produced without a cause; but by you it has been declared to be dependently arisen.
That which is dependent origination is itself considered by you to be emptiness;
"there is no independent entity"—this is your peerless lion’s roar.
The teaching of the nectar of emptiness is for the sake of abandoning all conceptual constructions;
yet you have brought down even that person who grasps at it.
O Protector, you have revealed that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature— inactive, powerless, empty, and arisen from conditions like an illusion.
Nothing whatsoever has been produced by you, nor has anything whatsoever been ceased;
as it was before, so it is after—you have awakened to suchness.
For without having relied upon this cultivation practiced by the noble ones,
how could the cognition of the signless ever arise here?
"You have stated that there is no liberation without having recourse to the signless;
therefore, you have demonstrated that [signlessness] in its entirety within the Mahāyāna."
Whatever merit I have acquired by praising you, the worthy object of praise,
who are free from the bonds of causal signs— by that may the entire world be liberated.
The *Śrīlokātītastava* is completed.
Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon, Stotra Section, Text No. 39:
*Lokeśvaraśatakam* (The Hundred Verses on Lokeśvara)
Om, homage to Lokanātha!
To the one whose crown bears the luster of radiant rubies, upon whose head the Lord of the Gods bows down.

May the splendors of the moon-like pure nails of the Lord of the World bring peace to the world— splendors that diminish the thick, tawny radiance of the crescent moon resting upon the head of Śambhu, appearing like a garland of blooming jasmine flowers upon his lotus-seated head bowed in devotion.
The darkness has certainly not been shaken off by the powerful rays of the moon on Śiva’s matted locks, which are dappled by contact with their tawny hue;
nor has it been dispelled by the intense luster of the rubies in Viṣṇu’s crown;
nor has it vanished into the mass of hair belonging to the gods who sport there, for it remains hidden within the very blackness itself.
May the irresistible splendors of the toenails of the Sovereigns of the World be for the pacification of your darkness.
It is the cause for the attainment of the full expansion of lotuses within the abundant and vast reservoirs;
it removes the fear of calamitous afflictions for those whose beloved ones have departed far away;
and even by its mere casting of waves, it pacifies the terror arising from the malignant influence of darkness.
May the unprecedented moonlight of the cool radiance from the nails on the feet of Lokeśa purify you.
May your lofty crests of flame— the great fire that utterly consumes the fuel of the mass of afflictions—
dispel the dense darkness of delusion bound within the three worlds through their playful radiance;
and may they become unfailing showers of the waters of nectar upon the masses of fire in the lands of hell.
The splendors of the multitude of his toenails, born from the feet of the Lotus-Bearer, destroy the cycle of existence.
Of those inconceivable wish-fulfilling gems, which are skillful in granting desires that cut off all self-will; which are enchanting in quelling the arising of intense fear and apprehension;
and which possess the luster of a mirror-image sustained by a multitude of various virtues clearly manifested, like the radiance of necklaces.
May the shadows of the nails of the feet of the Lord of the World, which possess upward-pointing rays, protect you.

May that mass of the luster of the Lord’s toenails— shining with the brilliance of his lofty, upward-pointing, and peerlessly beautiful crest-jewel, and itself radiant with its own splendor— long rise up for you,
towering high above the heap of beautiful jewels upon the heads of the gods who are expert in worshipping it.
The service of Śacī’s radiant bow was performed by a multitude of rays of light emanating in various ways.
Bestowing the attainment of desired objects upon those who serve them— thereby not failing in the elevation of glorious enjoyments—

they produce joy for their attendants with an unswerving luster on all sides; and by their stainlessness, they mock the moon with their incomparable reflections, having severed the defects of darkness.
May the nails on the feet of Padmapāṇi grant you satisfaction, like rubies serving as lamps.

May that sprout of the luster of the multitude of nails on the lotus-feet of the King of Kings— the sprout born from his lotus-feet— be the destroyer of the heavy burden of your intense fears of saṃsāra;
for it has arisen from the soil of his body, having bestowed its aid through an ocean of unceasing compassion.
He who has acquired the seed of consciousness, like a vast multitude of sprouts from the wish-fulfilling tree.
The rays from the toenails of the lotus-feet of Lokeśvara, which dispel the terror of the army of Śiva, possess the splendor of unerring arrows whose tips are fixed toward his red quiver;
they are like ropes constantly ready to rescue people fallen into the dreadful pit of saṃsāra.
May the ascending shoots cause you to reach the lofty state of great and difficult-to-attain prosperity.

Resplendent, heroic in severing the heat of the world rendered helpless by the exhaustion of afflictions and karma, teachers of keen intellect who perceive faults from afar— those stars that bestow intense bliss upon people, bearing the splendor of the full moon and remaining stainless.
May those inconceivable ones, whose lotus-hand nails are born from the feet, be victorious!
Is this an arrangement of worship made by Śambhu with fragments of the radiant crescent moon?
Or is it a string of jewels placed here by the Goddess of Enlightenment out of unsurpassed longing? Or perhaps it is a garland of divine and wondrous, incomparable flowers suspended by the gods?
May the thought, "May the row of [the Lord's] nails be pleasing," which was born from the feet of the Lord of the World, be for your benefit.

Where is this lotus-born [Brahmā], whose foot-dust has long rested upon the beds of the lofty rubies on the heads of bowing immortals; and where is this prostration with the crown of the head touching the surface of the earth?
Thus, as if bursting into laughter through their massed rays, those [rays] are formidable and difficult to endure.
May those nails of the Lord of the World, born from his feet, be for the destruction of darkness in the world.
They are heroes in the removal of heat, creating showers of the most cooling nectar-drops; they are ramparts against the destruction caused by the cruel and far-reaching torrent of fierce arrows;
[they are the remedy for] the manifold great sufferings within the vast belly of the prison-house that takes the form of saṃsāra.
May the splendors of the toenails of the glorious lotus-handed one, which bring prosperity, destroy your terrible [suffering].

The rays of light emanating from the toenails of the feet of Lokeśa produce the illusion of a curtain-like screen that obstructs the all-pervading arrows discharged by Māra, which are otherwise difficult to resist;
they are like a mass of great banners clearly portending the destruction of the army of afflictions.
Victorious are the great banners of victory, possessing powers impossible for the three worlds to withstand, which conquer the three realms of existence.
The mind of perfect enlightenment is like a mass of radiance shining forth like the moon;

it is like a great heap of ashes from the burnt-out fires of the afflictions, fanned by the wind of the vast path to liberation; and it is as indestructible as a slab of pure white stone set in place, unbreakable even by the cruel Māras.
May the mass of luster from the toe-nails of the lotus-handed one, imagined as [the rays] of the sun, protect you.

Those who for a moment must be gazed upon with embarrassment by the Lord of the Night (the Moon)— who is himself incapable of casting away the peerless darkness of his own misfortune due to the unimpaired waning of his phases— yet who possess stainless and inexhaustible vision; whose vows for the protection of the world, capable of destroying the factions of undiminished enemies, remain unbroken.
May those toenails of the Lord of the World protect you from being cast into the states of non-leisure.

May the incomparable exaltation of the mass of light from the nails of Him— He who is the means for attaining the six perfections, whose feet are the refuge of the preeminent lotus-bearer (Brahmā), and who desires to conquer the glory of the three worlds—
be yours; [an exaltation] which has clearly attained ultimate increase through its close association with the Friend (the Sun) that has risen.
May she protect [us], the cause for the great success of the Mahāyāna against all calamities, misfortunes, and enemies.
Shameless with his crest-lock, Paśupati bears at will the ornament of the crescent moon; the desire for beauty on the part of Viṣṇu is somehow extinguished by the Kaustubha gem of that fortunate one.
When he is seen, even that great crown of Indra’s crest-jewel becomes useless—so thought those whose minds were convinced.
May that multitude of toe-nails of the Lotus-handed One be victorious, whose luster was not even conceived by the worlds.
Rising high and far-reaching above, casting down its light upon the denizens of hell,
the moon— gleaming with the radiance of frost, pure, and the cause for the removal of the darkness from Rāhu’s face—
is of inscrutable power, providing a most clear vision for the entire world.
May the mass of rays from the nails of the lotus-feet resting upon the crown of the Buddha protect you!
Behold the mountain, radiant with the camphor powder released by the clever young wives of the joyful Lord of the Immortals as they worship;
its ground shimmering with the ashes from the matted locks of Śiva, who is inclined by the weight of his devotion;
and [dust] like the pollen from the tips of the filaments falling from the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī, scattered during her ritual offerings.
May the mass of rays from the nails of the hand and foot born from the lotus-holding one protect you from the lower realms.

The mass of light from the claws of the Lotus-Bearer’s lotus-feet— having drunk up the yellow luster [of the sun], possessing a crimson beauty like the thick dust of vermilion on the temples of the gods' elephants, having quelled the hero Śiva, having stolen the greenness from the horse of Indra, and having surpassed the brilliance of the serpent king— appears as a closing blue glow.
May he, watched by the wives of the gods who tremble at the swelling of the rising ocean of milk, protect you all.
"O Rambhā, beauty is already conceived in this [palanquin] by means of yak-tail fans as white as the moon;

why indeed do you scatter camphor powder in vain through the performance of your devotion? What need have you for these scattered flowers, pure as Śacī?"—thus was it said to you, the celestial nymphs, by your lord, the Lord of the Netherworld.
May the mass of light from the toenails of the Lotus-Handed One, described during his worship, protect you.

Upon the mountain Vindhya, which outshines Kailāsa, which has swallowed the blackness of the body of the Conqueror of Bali (Viṣṇu), which is anointed with the playful beauty of Kālī, and whose white rays from the sun’s horses have destroyed its greenness—
[the mountain] seems to have crumbled, as if thinking, "What can I do against this mass of rays from the great nails on the feet of the Lord of the World?"
May the moon protect you, appearing under the guise of a sacrificial pit crowded with gods and asuras skilled in worship.
The feet of the Buddha’s crown-nails,

which bear an exceedingly vast expanse and serve as a great bridge for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, are like water that quenches the great fire of rising, irresistible suffering through the accumulation of great merit.
May there be for you the instantaneous shattering of existence by that which possesses the brilliant flash of its own free will.
The eclipsing of the splendor of the moon beloved by Kālī; the mockery of the laughter of the radiance of the great mountain Kailāsa; the destruction even of the dignity of the Himalayan whiteness;
and the flooding of the quarters with the surges of the Ocean of Milk—even these are [the deeds] of the tusks of the celestial elephant.
May the expanse of the luster of the nails on the feet of Lokeśvara protect you—[a luster] that is a shadow of severance yet free from injury.

In that place, where the swarm of bees gathered in the *Pūjāpārijāta* tree closed their eyes upon the lotus of Śrī; where the Self-born One (Brahmā), intent on service, remained perched upon a budding lotus;
and by whom the day’s splendor was made dark and the night—whose fault of distressing the celestial damsels was quelled—was brought forth.
May that foot of Padmapāṇi, whose moon-like nails radiate shimmering moonlight, protect you all.
The beloved one, honored by the glances of the women of the gods whose husbands were bewildered,
bore a brilliant splendor arising from the luster of his nails like a cluster of white lotus stalks;
he was like a lover who, overcome by the expansion of manifold desires, has set out upon a solitary course.
May your foot, which is joyfully anointed with the sandalwood from the city of the gods, protect you—[the foot] of Padmapāṇi.

May Śrī bestow upon you supreme welfare— she who emerges from the midst of the milk-ocean of her stainless toenails, like the Kālīya serpent amidst a swarm of shimmering bees when the Pārijāta tree is scattered by the hands of the gods, which are radiant with the intense splendor of bliss.
Rising from the lotus-foot of Padmapāṇi, which is the cause of Acyuta’s delight.

May [the Lord]—whose splendor is concealed by the covering of bees that mimic the luster of lotuses; whose abundant clusters of blossoms are swollen with the rays of pure nails that expand freely and intensely; and who is the height of excellence in cutting away the flames of fire surging from the exhaustion of frustrated desires—be for your welfare.
May his foot, with the rays of its fingers anointed by the luster of a lotus, grant our desires effortlessly and without interruption.
Possessing the splendor of a wheel of emerging radiance, with the luster of stainless nails, he displays an incomparable glory arisen from a multitude of marks brought forth by immeasurable merit;
he is the great majesty arising from the lamp of all continents, the crown of the Buddhas.
May the foot of the sovereign of the world, which is worshipped by the crowns of all beings, protect you for a long time.
"What merit is there in this [hand] being strewn with the golden lotus-buds of the celestial Gaṅgā? What is the use of songs sung by swarms of bees, who mistake it for blooming lotuses?
"No," she replied, "it is possible for strings of rubies to shine upon these lustrous nails."
Victorious is that foot of the Lord of Gods, upon whose worship the hand of the one with busy lotus-like hands is ever engaged.
He who was indeed not even a cause for the birth of the Protector, the Sugata, among those possessing life;
in whom neither a swarm of bees nor even a person was partial in their longing for his lotus-feet;
by whom the three worlds, though already exceedingly heavy, were made to bow down further by him who is most venerable.
May that foot protect the world—the foot of the Sugata, whose crown is illuminated by the radiance of the moon.

May that Lord of the World, whose mass of pollen rests upon the heads of the immortals, long grant you prosperity— he who, by bestowing drink upon those who were not dejected, brought joy to his assembled servants; he in whom there was no lack of excellence, for he was indeed the very foundation for the ultimate beauty of his greenness.
The lotus-foot is the ground for the abode of prosperity and the highest good, its filaments laughing with the rays of light from the nails.

The invocation of the weapon [of your name] brings about the destruction of the bodies of embodied beings through fierce blows; it is the summoning for the attainment of their endeavors, yet it is the withdrawal of the exceedingly great majesty of those who have increased their own misfortune.
It is the burning of the fire of suffering caused by the great hostility produced by the performance of oblations of effort toward the hostile array of afflictions.
May the river of the army, which bestows manifold benefits, flow forth, possessing the state of lotus-hands and lotus-feet.

May the humming swarm of bees, wandering upon the flawless lotuses on the crown of the Buddha’s ornaments, eloquent yet beyond conceptual thought, bestow prosperity upon you as it glides toward his feet—
for the sake of establishing the singular task of protecting sentient beings in a state of most firm and long-enduring stability.
She was bound, as it were, by a heavy iron chain of abundant compassion.
With petals as beautiful as the inner leaves of a lotus, soft yet possessing the essence of a diamond,
it is the ground for the destruction of the multitude of weapons hurled by enraged enemies;
red in color, it is the cause of the supreme power that pacifies passion for the sake of crossing over.
May the foot of the Sugata, who bears the moon, be free from weariness for you within the ocean of saṃsāra.
Though fickle, she was not even capable of clinging out of restlessness to the cluster of lotuses blooming from the yawn of Indra;
nor, though restless, was she able to settle upon the mass of *kunda* flowers that bring joy to Śiva;
nor did she find delight in the radiant *pārijāta* tree before her, strewn with Viṣṇu’s garlands and fragrant with perfume.
May that lotus-foot of the Victor, where the swarms of bees delight, protect you all.
May he who is radiant with a mane shining from a mass of intensely risen splendor;
who is formidable with the luster of his upward-pointing claws and fangs suffused with a crimson glow;
and who is to be gazed upon by the tremulous, darting eyes of the fleeing enemies who are like elephants—be for your prosperity.
May the lion at the feet of Lokeśa, who reclines in the forest of the matted locks born from the lotus-born [Brahmā], be for our welfare.
Though clear, it was not clear; though light, it was not light for crossing the quarters of the sky;

though the delighter of the three worlds, it was the cause of intense, pervasive torment for others' bodies; though anointed with the ointment of beauty, it was exceedingly sweet, yet the suppressor of the affliction of distress.
May the radiance from the feet of the one who wears a crest-garland of blossoming flowers of Jina-like splendor bring you prosperity.
The King of Kings rejoiced with *rājīva* lotuses; Hari with green and captivating *pārijāta* trees; the Moon with *kunda* blossoms; Indra with radiant showers of abundant wealth;
and Varuṇa was pleased with *palāśa* flowers—thus the host of gods offered this distinguished and profuse worship.
May that foot of the Lotus-Handed One, which has been made to resemble poetry through its alliteration, protect you.

The sun, with his face turned upward toward her nails, offered praise at the blossoming of their luster; Indra was captivated by the tips of her fingers; and even Śiva and Antaka, though their eyes were fixed upon the joints of her limbs, were unable to behold the extraordinary excellence that lay within the range of her peerless beauty.
Victorious is that foot of the one whose crown is marked by the image of a Buddha, upon which the divine world rests without remainder.

May the foot of the Lotus-Bearing Mountain—whose form is a mass of thick, formidable matted locks brilliantly illuminated by the sun of the Perfectly Enlightened One; which acts as a pillar for the earth of the masses of people sinking in the ocean of saṃsāra; and which is served by the caravans of the Siddhas—be for your welfare.
May he, from whose mouth flows a great stream of the red mineral of luster vomited forth at the very end, protect you!

May the tree of the feet of the Lord of the World grant you prosperity—that tree which is the cause for the complete pacification of the exhaustion of all beings weary from the continuous journey of saṃsāra; which bears the fruit of fulfilling desires as its shade; whose branches are resplendent with the flowers of his radiant nails; and whose basin is the mass of garlands from the crowns of the gods who bow before it.
May the sprinkling of pure, radiant water from the jar filled with jewels, prepared at the root, bring about prosperity.

May that playful one protect you—he who has attained great joy from uprooting the powerful enemy force of the dense web of fundamental afflictions; he whose resplendent crown is the abode of the play of the Conqueror of Māra;
and he who, bearing the peerless, stainless lotus, is not deceived by the lure of blossoming lotuses.
He who delights in music that is surpassed by the swarms of bees fluttering about the abundant, trembling blossoms.
May he be the tethering post for the restless female elephant of the fortune of sovereignty over the three worlds;
the skilled bear (Rāhu) in protecting the entire universe when it falters from the bite of the serpent of painful affliction;
and the firm bolt on the gate of the city of hell, which is otherwise difficult to enter and lacks any defenses.
May the foot of the Lord of the World be for prosperity, the sole raft for crossing the ocean of existence.
Thus ended the instruction on the footstool; the manner of dancing ceased, and the faultless science of instrumental music was suddenly suspended.
Neither song nor even a lack of song was performed, nor were the aesthetic sentiments (bhāvas) brought forth by those who had composed the rasas.
Thus, in that assembly where Indra smiled within, the celestial nymphs (apsarases) were unable to perform their worship.
Victorious is that Lotus-Born One, who produces insatiable longing in those women afflicted by passion.
He who, through his unrestrained power and leftward path, crushes the pride of Māra as it meets him in conflict;
whose crown is immeasurable great splendor arising from the destruction of delusion at the center; who is formidable in his vast extent;
the glorious one of boundless abundance, equal in majesty to the Great Wish-fulfilling Tree in the realm of supreme plenitude.
May he, whose gentle mind is renowned for its boundless love for all beings, and who is the refuge of those without rest, be yours.

To him who, for those terrified by their torments, provides the refuge of remembrance within the belly of the prison— a place possessing formidable enclosures of solid walls and obstructions, and appearing like a city of hell with its cruel, vast, and terrifying barriers— [I bow].
May Lokeśvara, who acts with hospitality and possesses profound compassion, protect you in this world.

Leaping in the ocean— whose waters are noisy with rows of tossing waves stirred by the playful winds that blow at the end of an eon, and which are turbid and crowded with swarms of crocodiles— he took his stand, possessing the grace of one reclining upon the vast, pure, blue-lotus-studded floor of a palace.
May he, who is light-footed and dwells within the lotus, be capable of protecting the world.

The smoke rising from that [city], which binds the distressed moon with its mass of fumes, possesses a brilliance that rivals the persistent light of the sun; it is the foremost in uprooting the fortitude of the celestial wives who are bewildered by the obstruction and bursting forth of their sighs;
and even the fire itself assumes the form of a cloud as it bears the constant stream of the name of that [city].
May that Buddha-Holder, through his steadfastness, bring about for you a perfect and boundless destruction of all afflictions.

The lordly elephant, whose trunk was raised in rage with its tip curled like a dark iron weapon, emitting a cruel hissing sound, his massive body suddenly darkened as he was swarmed by bees clustering on temples moist with rut;
he who, when struck by the painful goad of the mere mention of your name, became wretched and fell into a state of cowardice.
May that Lord of the World, whose compassion provides all desired requisites, perform for you the work of fulfilling your every wish.

When the name of the enemy of the lord of venomous serpents enters the minds of those who are otherwise powerless, the biting snakes— whose mouths are revealed by their desire to bite, who are the fuel for the fire of wrath that consumes with the heat of poison, whose swelling is nourished by hissing breaths, and whose heads are violently raised— perish.
May he be the Lord of the World for the pacification of the extremely difficult mass of afflictions that is the refuge of the universe.

The lion, whose fierce speed was like a song for devouring herds of elephants seized by the heavy pride of their exuding ichor, who moved with impetuous strides and roared with deep resonance from the cavernous depths of his thick neck,
approached the assembly of vehicles through the application of the group's chanting.
May that yogi, whose supreme head is elevated and unattached to the Sugatas, ward off your misfortune.
Furthermore, that host— whose hearts were wounded by pity, who caused terror,

who was firm and comparable to mountains, and whose bodies had the luster of bees and gayals— having abandoned [the field], perished like a collection of illusions consisting of stratagems and spells; its valor having departed, it went to destruction.
May that abode of the Sugata, which is born from one who meditates upon his feet, lead to your victory.

The river of the enemy’s army— whose waters are the essence of the fuel for their incomparable battle— is a land of terror and habitation for fear, filled with the crocodiles of strife and greed, with waves breaking forth from the flashing brilliance of spears and lances, and possessing the foam of laughter in the form of outstretched, cool, and shimmering banners; yet it is crossed by the virtuous boat of service to him.
May that Lotus-Born One, moving with vigor through pleasure and pain, gather you together in happiness.

The thunderbolt, possessing the sovereign power to shatter the multitude of mountains, bearing the fire that is formidable with its vast consumption of the earth, and having become a source of bewildered terror for those overwhelmed by the excessive weight of existence,
fell swiftly upon the navel of the world as a ground of fear for those who possess dread.
By the power of whose devotion may he, who is as beautiful as a full-blown lotus, be the destroyer of worldly existence.

His fortitude shaken by afflictions, standing on the verge of death, pierced by the cruel sting of anger, his body oppressed by many various diseases difficult to endure due to the obstruction of pain—he whose mind was sustained by the application of meditation, which provided the nectar of supreme steadfastness— [The remainder of the verse continues: ...was not overcome by the host of enemies, nor did he fall into the power of the demon of death. (10) May that Blessed One, the Sage, who is the sole refuge for all beings, protect me. (11) I bow to him who is the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance, the lamp of wisdom, the sun of the Dharma, the moon of compassion, the king of physicians, the physician of the world, the healer of the world, the one who has transcended the world, the one who has crossed over the ocean of existence, the one who has reached the further shore, the one who has attained the state of peace, the one who has attained the state of liberation, the one who has attained the state of nirvāṇa, the one who is worthy of offerings, the one who is perfectly enlightened, the one who is the teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (12–14) I bow to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. (33) I bow to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksa
May he who possesses supernatural power, who is not subject to suffering, and whose head is the Buddha, protect your intellect for the sake of awakening.

The lord of the earth, whose fame for the suppression of enemies resounds through his incomparable majesty, who by his administration of justice has surpassed the renown of Yama, the Lord of the Dead, and who is himself the personification of *daṇḍanīti*—
even the wrathful-minded Bhūti attains great joy through the power of having studied at his feet.
May that abode of the bull-like Conquerors, which is the cause for the emergence of contradictions [in opposing views], remove your fear.

Brahmā was rendered speechless, even the Preceptor (Bṛhaspati) became a mere teacher, and Viṣṇu remained silent and daunted in the composition of words; even Śiva, though free from pride, was humbled.
Thus, it is clear that the gods were satisfied even while desiring to praise him, for they were not wise enough to describe his virtues.
Victorious is that glorious one, the lotus-hander, whose flood of virtues lies within the range of the Conqueror’s mind.

By the Creator, whose eyes are three, whose enemy is the foe of the gods (Śiva), and who is the friend of the mountains (the Himalayas)—by him, wondrous deeds were performed for the sake of his lineage; by his father, the preceptor of the world, his body was protected;
and by his son, who loves all the world as a mother would her child, his friendship was maintained.
May that Lord with the lotus in his hand, who is not attached to anything, protect you—he by whom this vessel of praise has been extolled.
In whom Brahmā found manifoldness, in whose various praises Skanda placed his own many heads filled with joy, and in whose act of salutation even the Lord of the Nagas bent his heads;
and whom the Three Worlds, upon beholding, caused Śakra to bring forth his ten hundred praiseworthy eyes—
May that Lord of the World, the worthy recipient of hymns of praise from those whose eyes never tire of gazing upon him, protect us.

The sun, whose rays are intensely blazing, indeed remains fruitlessly upon his path; yet the majesty of the Lotus-Bearer possesses a brilliance that brings light to the world. Thus, with an effulgence that inspires joy, the wise have offered praise to the assemblies of the court.
May that noble grace, which bestows swift favor upon enemies in this world, belong to him.

In that place where even a prostration is a supreme exaltation for those abiding in merit, and where honor toward the one of peerless and singular majesty is a great increase for those possessing devotion;
where even the mere remembrance of that site of meditation instantly causes the forgetting of fear of the elements.
May that Lord of the World, who has established the path of welfare in the infinite and inconceivable world, protect you!

The Indra-like thunderbolt of pride, which had previously shattered the enemies of the gods, became utterly exhausted; that captivating one, amidst rows of kings whose fears were rendered fruitless by his power, did not achieve his purpose with his discus—thus the people surely cried out, "It is Hari! O weapon! *Note: The final word *heti* is an exclamation of pain or distress.*
Victory to the lotus-born one, who delights the enemy hosts and is liberated from attachment to worldly expansion!
He who maintains a bliss transcending the world yet suffers with the intense suffering of the worlds;

who is eternally devoted [to others] yet remains ever without refuge for the wretched living beings; who is joined in yoga and is the sole lord of the three worlds, yet is intent on pleasing the people through his peerless beauty.
May he, whose head is crowned by the Perfectly Awakened One and who has performed inconceivable deeds unlike any other, long protect you all.

May that Lamp of Lokeśa be victorious in the world— the lamp whose application of incomparable affection is established throughout the three realms without interruption, which is unshakable by the powerful and heavy winds of the mad heretics, and which dispels the blinding darkness of delusion arisen within the mansion of the universe.
He is the destruction [of suffering] whose nature is indestructible, whose course is established through the exertion of performing benefit for others.
Where is this universal loving-kindness, and where is the burning enmity toward the thick and uneven afflictions?

Where is the mature power of liberation, and where is the firm binding of the noose of compassion? Where is the partiality of indifference, and where is the preoccupation with acting for the benefit of others? Such is its wonderful variety.
Wondrous is the conduct of the Lotus-Handed One; may it become for you a light that conquers even the world beyond.
Supreme among all, possessing a vast method for the manifestation of every form, the eternal protector of all,
he exists in every way for the sake of accomplishing the great and universal purpose of the Guru’s discipline;
by means of all his weighty qualities of majesty— which humble all pride— he subdues every arrogance.
May he who bestows everything upon you, the crown of all the omniscient ones, fulfill your vast aspirations.

"Lord, Master, Lord of Creatures, Preceptor of the Immortals, World-Guardian, Great Indra, Radiant One, Bestower of Punishment upon Enemies, Conqueror of the Strength of Foes, Giver of Wealth, and Holder of the Victorious Noose"—
thus did the attendants speak with names that were true to their meaning, while concealing a suppressed laugh within.
May that lotus-handed one be victorious, before whose alms-bowl the hosts of gods bowed down with unblushing devotion.

May that Saṃvara protect you—he who is the most excellent among the best of the noble; who dispels the distress of those seeking supreme boons; who bears immeasurable rays of light; who is difficult to be restrained by the hosts of irresistible and powerful enemies;
who is a hero who wards off heroic foes; and who possesses a vast, noble, and abundant mass of water.
May he be like a cloud that, through the pouring forth of a vast, wide-spreading, and copious stream of rain, is unable to withhold its downpour.
Perceiving that the entire world of living beings is like a traveler on the path of the ocean of saṃsāra, [the Lord]— who is ever-diligent, exceedingly powerful, and whose hand shines with the lotus—
became light by entrusting the burden [of the world] to him, and thus attained the state of the Lamp of the Universe, he who possesses great compassion.
May that Buddha—whose vow has been made fruitful and who maintains the support of steadfastness—grant you liberation.

Having ascended to a lofty height, he is weightier than the Sugata himself, bearing upon his hand the burden of the world’s manifold tasks as if it were his own noble ornament, Kamalā; and for those who possess devotion,
he has long brought the caravan of sentient beings to the extinction of the fires of hell, like a mass of cooling rain.
May he by whom the intense continuity of afflictions was pacified as if it were a person protect you.
He who, though renowned for his mastery in manifesting various infinite forms, is free from deceit;
who, though all fears have been stilled within him, acts with timidity out of extreme compassion;
and who, though devoid of anger, is constantly joined by the "wrath of the Buddha" for the sake of subduing those with malicious intentions.
Victorious is he whose crown shines with the Fully Awakened One; though the object of contemplation for the great, he is himself inconceivable.
He does not bear a head, but rather a supreme body beautiful with the light of Amitābha;

he has no lotus as a crest-ornament, for even the enemy host, distressed by great fear, is his ornament. Though occupied with destroying the world's enemies, he does not bind his matted locks into a topknot.
May that skillful Lord of the World protect you from the sight of the face of the enraged Yama.
The ocean of existence trembled, fearing for its remnants; the multitude of afflictions dissolved away;

and even the Sage, resting in peace, shone forth with the praiseworthy play of nirvāṇa, when he—having girded his loins—proceeded everywhere to perform deeds for the sake of all sentient beings without exception.
May he, whose crest-jewel is the abode of the Sugatas, thoroughly cleanse the stains from you through his exertion.
Thus ends the description of the Blessed One.

For the sake of destroying the world's enemies, Padmapāṇi [manifested] in an action that was difficult because it shattered the obstruction of the array of impediments, even on a ground where the mind finds no footing, and which cuts off absolute peace.

May that exceedingly weighty power of our Lord— by which one who is submissive, bought, or terrified acts without change of expression when commanded as if by a superior— protect you from the merciless Ender.

The ground is not subject to being surpassed, for even though it is exceedingly soft, it simultaneously and intensely illuminates infinite world-systems to pacify all fear; its splendor eclipses the entire brilliance of all luminous beings, rendering their light like a mere fraction of the glow of a firefly.
May Tejorlokeśvara remove from your hearts the dense darkness of worldly delusion.
Like a person who has filled all directions to their limit, the entire expanse of space was completely filled;

like the disappearance of all lights, the destruction of an unsurpassed mass of calamities began on every side; and together with the dense darkness, the Māra of great supernatural power and pride was brought to rest.
May that splendor of the one who bears the lotus arise for your prosperity; may it be born for you.

He is the Lord who destroys the light of others; the breaker of Bala, who is a fire to the mass of darkness that is difficult to endure for those with intentions hostile toward living beings; the infallible Acyuta, a wondrous sun whose power is capable of illuminating objects obstructed by various infinite mountains and other barriers.
May that single manifestation of Lokeśa, who resembles a host of immortals, be for the destruction of your fear.
Wherein there is the happiness of the desire for the abundant aquatic creatures— the perfected beings—
wherein the multitudes of heterodox teachers who cause harm to people sink downwards like mountains into that which is difficult to cross;
that [ocean] is irresistible on all sides, swelling with the intensity of the non-existence of the vast world-systems of existence.
May the ocean of the splendor of his lotus-like hand expand for you, in order to extinguish the fire of fear.

If the fire of hell is actually Nirvana, why [is it so]? If the flood of the nectar of Dharma is bound within the mass of matted locks for the sake of those to be trained, why [is it so]? If the Jina dwells as a venerable kinsman within the house of the head, why is the threefold world devoid of joy?
May this manifold conduct of the Protector, the Friend of the World, which is free from worldly attachment, destroy your [sins].
Though she is one, she manifests as many through the delightful diversity of forms fashioned by the power of the inclinations of sentient beings;
she is a thunderbolt-point of immense, shifting, and unshakable activity, difficult to pierce and consisting of unreal conceptualization.
She is the consort of Lokeśvara, the moonlight for the night-lotuses of noble wisdom, and the destroyer of the millions of calamities of the heretics.
May the teaching that destroys existence be like the sun that dispels the darkness, for your instruction.

This dispute, which is a locus for various rising controversies among proponents such as the followers of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda— abounding in intoxicants like the *durvāda* (evil speech) and *unmādana* (delusion)— is a contentious argument characterized by blame;
yet it is the destruction of the calamities of intoxicated people accompanied by pride, and the grace of the learned.
Victorious is the doctrine of the non-arising of phenomena, which is the very body of the Conqueror, crowned by the feet of the one who has attained perfection.

May that hand of the Lotus-Handed One stand as a refuge—his hand which has cast away the weapons of his enemies; whose mass of rays shines throughout the three worlds, dispelling the fear of those who tremble; whose multitude of rays is praised by the gods, which spreads wide like vast waters and utterly destroys the heat of those dwelling in the abode of the Maruts; and which wields the thunderbolt against Bala.
O you who are praised for the destruction of the fear that flourishes throughout the entire three worlds, may we not be abandoned!
Capable of uprooting the rows of lofty mountains and trees in regions ravaged by the shifting winds of cosmic dissolution, having his great pride severed,
he is the noble elephant of the Lord of the World, raining down a flood of ichor that attracts the bees of his devotees.
May you, whose hand is like an elephant’s trunk, be sufficient for the destruction of the city of the enemy that is worldly existence.
Possessing six treasuries and a storehouse, it has attained a state that fulfills the desired wish for the dense splendor of Buddhahood;
it possesses sharp edges that emulate a hundred-edged sword and have the honored power to terrify the wicked;
and it is never abandoned by the praise of virtues that serve as a dwelling place for the glory of perfect enlightenment.
May the lotus-hand of the Lord of the World be sufficient for you as the cause of liberation.
That lotus which dwells within the glory of awakening (*bodhilakṣmī*), which produces joy for the multitude of pretas distressed by the caverns of their throats agitated by ever-increasing thirst,
and which is the station of service to the virtuous for those who have fixed their minds on the desire for prosperity— that is the true lotus.
May that [lotus] of the Lord of the World, possessing a row of rows of brilliant clusters of radiant light, protect you all.

May that [Buddha], who causes people to resemble a parasol— protecting them from the sun of afflictions that intensely heats the dense mass of the spreading rays of manifold sufferings, and who produces those with dejected faces—
never fall into exhaustion, for he is the canopy of the sun that is no less than all the worlds.
May that stainless lotus, resting in the hand of Lokeśa, lead away your mental dejection.

The abode of power, the great source of majesty, the seat of splendors, the dwelling place of vastness, the refuge for the terror of enemies, the ground for the manifestation of the destruction of worldly fears arising from invincibility,
and the lovely, radiant, and tranquil home of that mass which expands with world-surpassing valor.
May the arm of Lokeśa be victorious, a fierce staff for the eradication of the harm inflicted upon many worlds.
Though it flows with a flood of the nectar of loveliness that causes only distress to his enemies, it never fails to grant satisfaction to the eyes;
it is a temple of beauty that eclipses all the ornaments of the entire world, yet itself serves as the ornament for all ornaments.
May that single robe, which by its abundance dispels both pleasure and pain, shine forth for you like the sun for the lotus.

In this ocean of loveliness, where the eyes of the meritorious— once withered by pride in their own beauty— have attained fulfillment in the world, yet are struck down by those excessively restless with craving,
I believe it must have been rendered incomparable by countless other radiant beings, such as the Moon and others.
If even one of his eyes were to surpass that of the lotus-handed one, then let his face be victorious.

In that [place], for those who harbor enmity, there occurred repeatedly and most clearly a scorching foul weather, produced by clouds of the flood of water consisting of their incessantly shimmering splendor; yet for embodied beings,
the continuous smears of thick ink-stain and the persistence of their bonds were washed away and destroyed.
May that temple, facing upward and bestowing supreme bliss, perform various wondrous deeds for you.
Of him whose hands are untainted by desired lotuses, who sits upon the edge of a clearly defined and vast jeweled floor,
whose excellence of luster is pale-red due to the intense mass of light from Amitābha closely embraced [by him],
and whose dense construction of the upper part is unseen because it is pervaded by beauty— [he possesses] a binding of fierce majesty.
May the armor [of the Buddha], which is the friend of the pungent *kaṭa* tree amidst the dense thicket of his unchanging and guileless matted locks, protect you.

Sprinkled by the continuous and vast flow of the water-like radiance of Amitābha— the cause of ultimate delight— he attained growth, becoming exceedingly beautiful through his stainless purity; he was honored with heaps of divine, wondrous flowers of unrestrained fragrance, which fulfill all desired aims.
May that mass of wish-fulfilling creepers which are the matted locks of Nalinadhara stand for your attainment of perfection.
Those upon whom the Lord Amitābha, having cast off his other dwelling, bestows liberation when bound and an extraordinary adornment through his body when released;
those who destroy all worldly fragrance and anoint every quarter with incomparable, intense perfume.
May those dreadlocks of yours, like the consorts of the world-protectors, remove death—which is inevitably encountered and exceedingly terrible—from you.
Her matted locks are not a mass of snares for binding the minds of all people;
her loveliness is not a flood of nectar that sustains the lives of the world when it is distressed by the fire of suffering;
nor is she a lotus that dispels the faults of affliction, like a whip for the horse of the wicked one who brings destruction.
May the Lord whose hair is entwined with the moon of the Jina grant you the fulfillment of your cherished hopes and prosperity.

With his lips bitten and his evil gaze blazing, he resembles the fire of cosmic destruction, eager to swallow the three worlds in its impetuous fury, terrifying all who are distressed by the delusion of a world set ablaze by the spreading, unrestrained, and tawny radiance of his splendor; yet he is gazed upon with fixed devotion by Lakṣmī.
May the gaze of the World-Mistress, born for you and momentarily distressed by incomparable compassion, protect you.
Today the world clearly goes to ruin; all the great mountains swiftly turn to dust, and even the infinite oceans go dry—
such is the fate from the forehead of Him, which has become terrifying with the contraction of the frown of Death.
May he be victorious, who, seeing the Goddess departing, [protected] the lotus-born one who was terrified by his incomparable strength of arm.
May she who is praised with hymns by those worthy of praise, who is herself the Guru of even the Gurus in this world and is worshipped by those worthy of worship;
who, as if personified, possesses the sincere power to protect the entire universe acquired over many kalpas;
and who, like the lotus-born Brahmā, has emerged from incomparable compassion itself to sever the suffering of the world—may she be present.
May Tārā, who removes the heavy, shimmering causes of bondage within the belly of the prison of saṃsāra, protect you!

His multitude of qualities is sung by the assembly of gods; he is to be grasped by those who stand before the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati); he is profound with a clear movement through the non-dense spheres; he is traversed by swans with fierce strides;
his greatness is proclaimed by those who utter deep resonances; and he possesses but a small portion of the mass of things that can be sung.
May the entire flood of virtues of the Victorious One, who is rightly to be attained, protect you—those virtues which are the lotus-born from the words of the Sugata.
May I too, in birth after birth, be a devotee at the feet of Avalokiteśvara,
possessing a nature that takes refuge in the supreme wisdom, and one who makes the welfare of others his primary task.
The *Śrīlokeśvaraśataka*, composed by the great minister Śrīvajradatta, is hereby completed.

I worship the auspicious Śrī Lokanātha, the wise one who bestows blessings; he who possesses manifold forms, is a man of merit, and is the refuge of the world; who necessarily assumes the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; who enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra, and whose eyes are as long as lotuses.

I worship the divine Śrīlokanātha, the bestower of auspiciousness, who provides protection for all people afflicted by fear; whose face is lovely, whose ears are graced with beautiful golden earrings, and who shines with jeweled ornaments such as necklaces.

I worship that auspicious and wise Śrī Lokanātha, whose forehead-mark is of the nature of intense heat, who is a mine of jewels for the gods, whose hands are beautified by golden spears, who is radiant, the bestower of directions through the wearing of ornaments, and the granter of well-being.

I worship the divine Śrī Lokanātha, the bestower of auspiciousness, who removes foul odors and miserable rebirths, who takes away misfortunes, who brings about the destruction of famine, who is a mine of compassion, a granter of knowledge, a treasury of virtues, and possesses a body that is beautiful and pure.
Thus I worship the auspicious Śrī Lokanātha, the divine one who bestows blessings, the lord of all hosts of beings, the sovereign of the three worlds who is praised even by the immortals,
and who has thus comfortably entered his excellent chariot in a certain place.

I worship the glorious Lord of the World, the wise one who bestows auspiciousness, who is bowed to by all— by yakṣas, kinnaras, humans, sages, nāgas, vidyādharas, hosts of gods, danujas, and piśācas— and who is saluted with joined palms by the planets.

With my limbs beautifully adorned by the application of perfumes such as sandalwood, musk, excellent camphor, saffron, and yellow sandalwood, I worship the glorious Lokanātha, the divine one who bestows auspiciousness.

I worship the wise Śrī Lokanātha, the bestower of auspiciousness, whose excellent name destroys diseases and the like for those who take refuge in him; who removes sorrows and other sufferings; who is to be meditated upon for the sake of happiness; whose speech is like nectar; and whose body is born of gentleness.

I worship the glorious Lord of the World, the wise one who bestows auspiciousness; his arms hang down to his knees, his waist is like that of a lordly elephant, his head is the pinnacle of a pool of beauty, his teeth are as beautiful as crystal, his body is exceedingly handsome, and his limbs possess the marks of excellence.
Those people who, being sincere in nature, always recite this fragrant hymn to the Lord of the World—
Śrī Lokanātha himself, grasping it with his own hand, swiftly grants their desired aims.
The *Śrīlokeśvarastotra* is completed.

*Madhyamakaśāstrastutiḥ* (Praise of the Treatise on the Middle Way)

The ninefold teaching, beginning with the sūtras, which was proclaimed here by the Buddhas according to the conduct of worldly beings, skillfully relying upon the two truths, has been composed by the master Candrakīrti.
When passion has been dispelled, no talk arises regarding the destruction of hatred;
when hatred too has been dispelled, no talk arises regarding the destruction of passion.

Even that teaching which leads to the destruction of pride and the like does not destroy other defilements; therefore, it is not all-pervasive, and yet there are various other discourses of great significance therein. But this discourse for the total destruction of delusion [destroys] all afflictions without exception.
For all afflictions spoken of by the Victors are said to be destroyed when one relies upon non-delusion.

Furthermore, since dependent origination and the like have been taught for the sake of the complete destruction of this delusion, that very reality is its antidote; it is proclaimed by the Sugatas as the Middle Way.
And since the Sage’s body consists of the Dharma, it is therefore called emptiness.
It is proclaimed as the heart of the Buddhas and as the Great Vidyā.
Since this [emptiness] has arisen as the source of all qualities, it is for that reason described at great length and primarily in the *Madhyamaka* treatise by the Buddhas;
having understood the teaching exactly as it is, with a mind melted by compassion.
By that wise son of the Buddhas, Nāgārjuna, with reverence.
The teaching of the Jina is profound; indeed, no person understands it, for those who desire to declare the reality as something distinct from the words of the Lord of Munis,
and others who, being of inferior intellect, explain the scripture otherwise, do not know it.
And by refuting those as well, this treatise has been composed, having destroyed the two internal extremes.
It is clear that Nāgārjuna, accompanied by Rāhulabhadra and with his words followed even by the King, lived for a long time;
having defeated all the non-Buddhist heretics whose intellects were certain through their discernment of his treatises—
The disciples of Sthavira also proclaimed the teaching of the Best of Sages for a long time.
When the son of the Victor, Nāgārjuna— who had compassionately cut off and given his own head to a beggar seeking a head who had arrived— had departed for Sukhāvatī,
the treatises he composed and his assembly of disciples also met with destruction after a long period of time.
Now that the sun of reality has set, that doctrine is no longer clearly evident anywhere.
Nowadays, in this world, when the Buddhist doctrine has mostly strayed far from the true path— being skilled only in the mere fabrication of fanciful meanings, intoxicated by the wine of logic,
and agitated while lacking the realization of the reality taught by the Omniscient One— [how can one find peace?]
Blessed is he who, casting aside even for a moment all wrong views, plunges into emptiness.
He who, though bound by the snares of the scriptures composed based on objective entities out of fear,

leaps up with the spirit of a philosopher and goes beyond the moat of those very objects— he alone is that great deer; I have no concern for him today, for I possess only one quality which he lacks now.
It is precisely for that purpose that I have composed this commentary, which crushes other treatises.
Having studied for a very long time with diligence the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, the *Parikathā*, the *Ratnāvalī*, the *Saṃstutis*, and those *Kārikās* spoken in the treatises,
as well as the *Yuktyākhyā*, the *Ṣaṣṭikā*, the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*, and that *Śūnyatāsaptati*;
And that which was composed for the sake of the disputation, intended to turn [the opponent] back—that too [he refuted].
Having seen that manifold and profound sūtra, such as the *Śataka* and others, as well as the commentary composed by Buddhapālita, which is subtle and intended for those of future generations,
and whatever has been obtained by me through investigation from the traditional lineage;
Having summarized all this, it has been set forth for the satisfaction of those with exalted intellects.

This Cintāmaṇḍala, the crusher of sophistry, now stands manifest here, illuminating with the rays of his speech the objects of knowledge that are directly present, correctly and without confusion for those of sharp intellect; and bestowing this most lucid commentary, the illustrious Candra now shines with fame.
Having arisen for the worlds, it destroys misconceptions along with the dense darkness.
Having respectfully composed this orderly treatise on the correct ritual procedure—
which relies upon both reasoning and scripture for the sake of establishing certainty among the faithful and the wise—
whatever vast merit I have gained, may the entire world, like emptiness itself, [attain liberation] by that alone.
Having abandoned the multitude of views, may one proceed upon the path that cuts through all conceptual proliferation.
Having prostrated to the Teacher Gautama, to the perfectly awakened Buddhas who abide in that very nature of reality, to the entire host of the Conqueror’s sons, and to the Dharma spoken by them—
which serves as the eye for embodied beings in the perception of the infinite words of the Buddha— [I shall compose this work].
I pay homage to that Nāgārjuna who, out of compassion, composed this Madhyamaka.
The *Madhyamakaśāstrastuti* composed by Śrī Candrakīrti is completed.

Sattvārādhanagāthā (Verses on Pleasing Sentient Beings)

The work composed by the noble Nāgārjuna remains with me solely for the sake of sentient beings; faith in sentient beings resides in me and nowhere else, for alas, I am one who has taken sentient beings as his own.
Any practice that is devoid of compassion would be base; it is through compassion alone that such [base practice] is abandoned.
He whose engagement in compassion toward sentient beings is absolute is one who honors my teaching and knows its vital points;
he who possesses constant virtue, learning, compassion, and wisdom is alone declared to be a performer of worship for the Sugata.
For the sake of performing what is wholesome, I have gone to attain perfection; I carry this body solely for the benefit of sentient beings.
If I were not to act thus for the welfare of beings, I would make the nourishment of this body with food and drink entirely in vain.

How can he who harms sentient beings even in his mind rely upon me, when he is indifferent toward me? Yet that which brings satisfaction to the mind of the one worthy of worship—even if it consists merely in looking to the welfare of sentient beings—constitutes true worship.
Worship that is violent in nature or arises from the harming of others does not truly accord with the object of worship, even if it is elaborately performed.
It leads away one's wife, children, wealth, greatness, kingdom, and even the body, which is composed of flesh, blood, and marrow.
"Whatever I have renounced on account of their dearness—whosoever harms them, by him I am harmed.
For my supreme worship consists in being intent upon benefiting sentient beings; and through being intent upon harming sentient beings, there would be my defeat."
Having encountered sentient beings, I have performed virtuous deeds and propitiated the Protectors;
and while remaining dedicated solely for the sake of the assembly of sentient beings, I have attained the perfections.
With a mind exerted for the welfare of sentient beings, the power of Māra was shattered.
It was by sentient beings themselves, through their various actions, that I was fashioned such that I became a Buddha.
Upon what object can compassion and loving-kindness be established here? Upon what can they take their support?

What is the objective domain for equanimity, sympathetic joy, and the rest? Upon what are the liberations and so forth directed? For whose sake has patience been cultivated for a long time by one whose mind is intent on compassion?
Were it not for friends who act with kindness in birth after birth, living beings would not exist.
It is sentient beings alone who, having entered into states such as elephants and so forth, have been given by me on countless occasions;

and it is sentient beings alone who, having become worthy recipients, have been made to accept what was to be given by me. Because sentient beings themselves undergo various states of existence, my compassion has been increased.
If I do not protect sentient beings themselves, for whose sake would any purpose have been accomplished?
If living beings had not become habituated to the world of Yama through the mockery of the whirlpools of birth in this saṃsāra, which abounds in calamities and blows,
then this most wonderful and magnificent majesty of the Sugata— the crossing over from saṃsāra— would not exist.
For whose sake would there be any striving, if sentient beings were not dear to me?
"As long as this teaching of mine, which illuminates the world, endures, so long must you— who are self-possessed and devoted to the welfare of others— remain,
tirelessly hearing and practicing what I have composed for the sake of sentient beings."
You should not feel weary, nor should you disregard this body which has been stripped of its essence.
The Verses on Pleasing Beings, spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One, are completed.
